León, de 71 años, explicó a los peregrinos reunidos en la Plaza de San Pedro para su oración dominical semanal que el nódulo estaba "bien localizado" y se había detectado a tiempo, y les pidió que oraran "por la visita pastoral que voy a realizar" a Uruguay, Argentina y Perú. "Recientemente, durante unos exámenes médicos, los médicos encontraron un nódulo localizado en mi pulmón", dijo el pontífice. "Se detectó en una fase muy temprana y está bien localizado". "Los médicos consideran aconsejable intervenir, por lo que, siguiendo su consejo, he decidido someterme a una intervención quirúrgica para extirparlo", añadió. "La operación ya está programada para los próximos días". Un nódulo pulmonar es una pequeña lesión localizada que puede ser benigna. Según la Sociedad Torácica Americana, menos del 5% de los nódulos pulmonares resultan ser cancerosos, aunque el riesgo aumenta con la edad, el tamaño y otros factores. Leo, elegido papa por los cardenales de todo el mundo en mayo de 2025, es más joven de lo usual para ser jefe de la Iglesia. Le gustan los deportes, entre ellos el tenis, y no se tiene constancia de que haya tenido problemas de salud antes. Su predecesor, el difunto papa Francisco, falleció a los 88 años y se encontraba cada vez más débil en sus últimos años. La oficina de prensa del Vaticano indicó que se esperaba que la recuperación de Leo tras la intervención quirúrgica durara aproximadamente una semana. No facilitó de inmediato más detalles sobre el estado de salud del papa. Leo tiene una agenda muy apretada y tiene previsto realizar una gira de 11 días por Uruguay, Argentina y Perú del 6 al 17 de noviembre.

item.title: Pope Leo says he will undergo surgery for small growth on lung
item.description: Pope Leo said on Sunday that doctors had detected a small growth on his lung during a recent health check and he would be undergoing surgery this week to remove it, in the first health scare of the 71-year-old pontiff's tenure.
item.dc:creator: Joshua McElwee
item.content:encoded: Pope Leo said on Sunday that doctors had detected a small growth on his lung during a recent health check and he would be undergoing surgery this week to remove it, in the first health scare of the 71-year-old pontiff's tenure. Leo told pilgrims in St. Peter's Square for his weekly Sunday prayer that the growth, a small nodule, was "well-contained" and had been spotted early. The Vatican did not say whether the nodule is believed to be malignant. "Recently, during some medical examinations, doctors found a localized nodule in my lung," said the pontiff. "It was detected at a very early stage and is well contained." "The doctors believe it is advisable to intervene, so, following their advice, I have decided to undergo surgery to remove it," he said. "The operation is already scheduled for the next few days." A nodule on the lung is a small, localised lesion that can be benign. The American Thoracic Society says fewer than 5% of lung nodules overall prove cancerous, although risk rises with age, size, and other factors such as smoking. "Lung nodules are fairly common and are often benign," said Stephen Liu, a lung cancer expert at Georgetown University in Washington and division chief of hematology-oncology at MedStar Georgetown University Hospital. "When there is sufficient concern, and when it is safe to do so, based on the location of the nodule and the overall health of the patient, surgical removal can provide a definitive diagnosis," he said. LEO A RELATIVELY YOUNG POPE, PLAYS SPORTS Leo, elected pope by the world's cardinals in May 2025, is relatively young for a Church leader. He enjoys sports, including tennis, and is not known to be a smoker or to previously have had health issues. Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni wished the pope well. "I would like to express to the Holy Father my personal support, and that of the Italian government, as he faces this challenge in the coming days," she said in a statement. "The serenity and composure with which he spoke about it (today) ...are reassuring," Meloni added. The late Pope Francis, Leo's predecessor, died at age 88. He was hospitalised several times as he grew frail in his later years. He did not usually announce his hospital visits in advance, sometimes sparking a media frenzy over his health. The Vatican press office said Leo's recovery from surgery was expected to take about a week. It did not immediately provide further details about the pope's health. Leo keeps a busy schedule and is due to make an 11-day tour of Uruguay, Argentina and Peru from November 6-17. Before mentioning his health issue in his address on Sunday, the pope referred to the trip, thanking Catholics for their prayers "for the pastoral visit I will undertake."

item.title: At least 139 migrants dead, including some children, after boat from Djibouti to Yemen capsizes, UN agency says
item.description: At least 139 migrants, including at least 15 children, have died and around 84 are missing after a boat carrying more than 300 people capsized while sailing from Djibouti to Yemen, the United Nations' International Organization for Migration said on Sunday.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: At least 139 migrants, including at least 15 children, have died and around 84 are missing after a boat carrying more than 300 people capsized while sailing from Djibouti to Yemen, the United Nations' International Organization for Migration said on Sunday. The boat, carrying 305 people, capsized near Guhere, north of Obock — a port town in Djibouti — during the night of October 8-9, the IOM said, citing survivor accounts. Around 82 people survived the shipwreck, the statement said. A spokesperson for the Ethiopian government did not immediately respond to requests for comment. Photographs shared by the UN agency showed worn-out sandals and sneakers washed up on the shore. "Our teams are on the ground alongside local authorities to provide emergency assistance," said IOM Chief of Mission in Djibouti Alexandre Coissac. "This tragedy is a stark reminder of the dangers faced by migrants along this migration corridor as they seek economic opportunities," Coissac said. Djiboutian authorities are continuing search and rescue operations, the IOM statement said, adding that local authorities are also providing medical care to survivors and arranging burials for the deceased. The Djibouti government could not be immediately reached for comment. The migrants were heading to Yemen, with the hope of eventually making it to wealthier Gulf nations, even as Yemeni nationals themselves [USN:L6N45E0CP TEXT:"flee their country"], which is [USN:L6N45T0PU TEXT:"experiencing"] the most serious escalation in fighting between Saudi Arabia-backed government forces and the Iran-backed Houthis since a UN-brokered truce in 2022. "Despite the violence in Yemen, migrants are still making the perilous journeys hoping to make it to the Gulf countries," the IOM statement said. FIGHTING IN ETHIOPIA Fighting has also broken out in Ethiopia since last month in the [USN:L6N45W02E TEXT:"biggest escalation of violence"] since the 2020-2022 Tigray war. An IOM official told Reuters that the UN agency had documented heavy migrant traffic along the so-called Eastern Route through Djibouti for several years. "People continue to use the route amid changing conditions in Ethiopia and Yemen, although the volume and direction of movement can shift over time," the official said. Ethiopian migrants interviewed as part of the agency's most recent situation report on Djibouti from September 20 to September 30 said they had left their country due to difficult living conditions, including the impact of drought. "Some migrants also reported that they were fleeing conflict and forced recruitment by armed forces," the report said. Multiple residents of Tigray, where fighting erupted on September 23, have told Reuters that they had seen Tigrayan rebels forcibly recruit young men into the defence forces. The rebels have denied conducting forced recruitment. The conflict has sparked fears of a return to all-out war with Ethiopia and Eritrea severing relations over alleged Eritrean support for the rebel alliance seeking to overthrow Ethiopia's government. Eritrea has denied backing the alliance. SEVERE RISKS The so-called Eastern Route presents many dangers, including accidents at sea, trafficking and arbitrary arrests once on land. In 2025, more than 900 migrants died or went missing along the route, according to IOM’s Missing Migrants Project, as the number of people undertaking the journey increased by 18%. IOM has described the crisis sparked by the fighting in Yemen as alarming, with displacement figures surging to 200,000 from 76,000 in mid-September, according to data released by the agency last week. More than 3,700 people have fled Yemen by sea to Djibouti as of last week, it said.

item.title: Saudi Arabia reports injuries in new attack at Riyadh airport, day after strike kills 13
item.description: The attack comes a day after the deadliest strike on the kingdom in more than a decade killed 13 people and wounded more than 300 at the airport.
item.dc:creator: Jana Choukeir, Maha Dahan, Timour Azhari, Yasmine Ghania
item.content:encoded: Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthis claimed responsibility for Saturday's strike on Riyadh's international airport that killed 13 people and wounded more than 300, as Saudi authorities reported people were injured in a new attack on the airport on Sunday. The Saudi-led coalition in Yemen said an "unidentified projectile" had targeted Riyadh's international airport Terminal 4 on Sunday, causing a fire. An unspecified number of people were injured, the Saudi civil aviation authority said, adding it was still assessing the damage. The coalition also said Saudi air defences had intercepted a cruise missile in the vicinity of King Khalid International Airport. The strikes have exposed vulnerabilities in Saudi defence capabilities as the kingdom wages an air campaign against the Houthis to support a ground war in Yemen by the Yemeni government against the Iran-aligned group. The airport has been closed since Saturday's attack. However, a long-planned international energy conference went ahead in Riyadh on Sunday as planned. HOUTHIS CLAIM RESPONSIBILITY FOR OTHER ATTACKS In a televised speech on Sunday, Houthi military spokesperson Yahya Saree claimed responsibility for Saturday's attack and also said the group had attacked the airport in Dammam in Saudi Arabia's Eastern Province and two facilities of Saudi oil giant Saudi Aramco (2222.SE) . There was no immediate Saudi confirmation. Reuters has reached out to the Saudi media office and to Aramco for comment. The Houthis earlier on Sunday had renewed their warning to airlines, airport workers, and travellers against using Saudi airports. "We urge everyone to take our warnings seriously, and Saudi Arabia bears responsibility for any failed interceptions," the group said. 'WORSE IS YET TO COME,' HOUTHIS WARN Saudi Arabia has stepped up its military involvement in Yemen in recent weeks, launching strikes against the Houthis and backing a Yemeni government counteroffensive after the group seized strategic territory along the Red Sea coast last month. The Houthis said on Sunday that Saudi Arabia carried out 124 air strikes in Yemen in the past 24 hours, including the capital Sanaa and the group's stronghold Saada. Yemen's Houthi-run foreign ministry said that further Saudi military action in Yemen would trigger a stronger response, adding that its actions would be guided by the principle of reciprocity. "Unless the Saudi enemy stops its aggression and interference in Yemen, worse is yet to come, God willing," the ministry said in statements carried by Houthi-run Al Masirah television. US President Donald Trump said on Saturday the United States was considering joining Saudi strikes on the Houthis in the conflict, a spillover from the wider war on Iran that the US and Israel launched in February. INTERNATIONAL ENERGY CONFERENCE STILL GOING AHEAD The five-day conference of international energy organizations WPC Energy opened as planned on Sunday at a convention centre some 10 km (6 miles) from the airport. Meanwhile, a ministerial meeting of the International Energy Forum also went ahead on Sunday, with its plenary session to be held behind closed doors, according to a media advisory. No further details were immediately available and it was not clear which ministers joined the meeting. Italy's energy minister, Gilberto Pichetto Fratin, whose country was co-hosting the event, had said on Friday he would participate remotely via video link. German officials were trying to organise a return flight for Economy Minister Katherina Reiche, who was in Riyadh to attend the WPC conference and ministers' meeting. She was supposed to return to Berlin on Monday but the ministry said it appeared likely that her flight would not be able to take off due to the closure of the airport and alternatives were being considered. Separately, Saudi authorities notified parents that in-person classes at all schools in Riyadh would be suspended and shifted to remote learning from Sunday until Thursday for all students, teachers and administrative staff. In Saturday's attack, the third on Riyadh's airport in a week, the dead included four Saudis, two Bangladeshis and nationals of the United States, Jordan, Palestine, Syria, Sudan and Egypt, Saudi authorities said. India's embassy in Riyadh said on Sunday one of its citizens injured in the attack had died, adding to the initial death toll of 12. Four people were killed in the two previous attacks on the airport earlier in the week. One of the attacks also caused heavy damage to a Saudi commercial plane parked on the tarmac.

item.title: Smith sets catching record as Australia take firm grip on test
item.description: Australia's Steve Smith set a record for most test catches as his side finished the third day of the first test with a 139-run lead over hosts South Africa before bad light brought an early close to Sunday's play at Kingsmead.
item.dc:creator: Mark Gleeson
item.content:encoded: Australia's Steve Smith set a record for most test catches as his side finished the third day of the first test with a 139-run lead over hosts South Africa before bad light brought an early close to Sunday's play at Kingsmead. Smith took four superb catches to take his test tally to 223, going past the record of 220 held by England's Joe Root. Two of the catches showed outstanding anticipation as Smith shuffled across a few steps to snag South Africa captain Temba Bavuma and Kyle Verreynne as they both tried reverse sweeps off the spin bowling of Nathan Lyon. He also produced a flying dive across first slip to break the record and see off the threat of David Bedingham. His last catch, off Beau Webster, brought South Africa’s innings to a close as they scored 284 in reply to Australia’s first innings of 390. At stumps, Australia were 33 without loss in their second innings with Nic Maddinson 17 not out and Travis Head scoring 10. Smith’s heroics were in contrast to his last test appearance in South Africa eight years ago when he was captain of the team embroiled in a ball-tampering scandal and handed a one-year ban. But the sparse home crowd on Sunday were reminded of the 37-year-old’s skills as he contributed to his side’s handy lead with some extraordinary athleticism. South Africa face an uphill battle if they are to salvage something from the test with two days’ play remaining. Their batsmen were guilty of playing loose shots at crucial junctures after resuming the day 27-1 with three wickets falling before lunch, four more in the second session but the last two adding 87 runs before the innings came to a close. "Every time we looked like getting something going, we lost a wicket and that set us back a bit," said South Africa batting coach Ashwell Prince. Bedingham top scored with 49 but, like most of his teammates, got out to a rash shot. His was a thick edge off a back-foot drive to a Pat Cummins delivery that saw Smith dive across first slip like a top goalkeeper to snag the ball. Other batting contributions came from Aiden Markram, who made 37, and tail-enders Simon Harmer (35 not out) and Keshav Maharaj with 34. Cummins returned figures of 3-54, with two wickets each for Josh Hazlewood, Mitch Starc and Lyon. "There is still a long way to go but we hope that in the South African second innings, the pitch will deteriorate," said Lyon, whose spin could prove key to the outcome of the game. All three days of the test have ended early because of bad light stopping play, and extra time will again be added to all three of Monday's sessions.

item.title: Indonesia moves 8 endangered orangutans to safety after Borneo fires
item.description: Indonesian authorities and conservation workers successfully moved eight orangutans to a safe location after the endangered primates' homes were destroyed by wildfires in the forests of Borneo, they said on Sunday.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: Indonesian authorities and conservation workers successfully moved eight orangutans to a safe location after the endangered primates' homes were destroyed by wildfires in the forests of Borneo, they said on Sunday. The Southeast Asian nation is battling its most intense wildfires in 11 years, mainly on Sumatra and Borneo islands, and the government has warned the blazes could continue until November, aggravated by the El Niño weather pattern. Three mother-child pairs and two adolescent male orangutans were among those rescued between August and September from several locations, the Indonesian government and wildlife foundation, Yayasan Inisiasi Alam Rehabilitasi Indonesia (YIARI) said in a statement. "Their relocation to Batu Nyambu protected forest is expected to give the eight orangutans a chance to return to living naturally," the statement read. Orangutans are critically endangered great apes found in the wild only on the Southeast Asian islands of Borneo and Sumatra, with Indonesia home to all three recognised species, according to the World Wildlife Fund. Populations have declined due to deforestation, wildfires and poaching. The relocation operation took six hours by car, one hour on boats, and two more hours on foot, with the orangutans in cages carried on bamboo poles. Before they were moved, YIARI conservationists checked the animals' health. Since August, the West Kalimantan Natural Resources Conservation Agency and YIARI have rescued 46 orangutans affected by fires, agency head Murlan Dameria Pane said. From January to July this year, fires burned around 202,000 hectares (500,000 acres) in Indonesia. No official data for subsequent months has been released, but non-governmental organisations estimate fires have burned at least 600,000 hectares more since. Haze from the fires has caused 175,000 cases of respiratory illness in Indonesia, with the smog affecting neighbouring Singapore and Malaysia where many schools were closed on Friday as air quality deteriorated.

item.title: Ukraine-Trump annonce un cessez-le-feu dans l'énergie, Zelensky attend des précisions
item.description: Le président américain Donald Trump a annoncé dimanche la conclusion d'un accord de cessez-le-feu entre l'Ukraine et la Russie portant sur les infrastructures énergétiques et son entrée en vigueur, avant d'être rapidement contredit par son homologue ukrainien Volodimir Zelensky.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: Le président américain Donald Trump a annoncé dimanche la conclusion d'un accord de cessez-le-feu entre l'Ukraine et la Russie portant sur les infrastructures énergétiques et son entrée en vigueur, avant d'être rapidement contredit par son homologue ukrainien Volodimir Zelensky. "Avec effet immédiat, il y a un CESSEZ-LE-FEU ÉNERGÉTIQUE dans la guerre entre la Russie et l'Ukraine. Les deux parties ont donné leur accord. Ne le violez pas !", a écrit Donald Trump sur son réseau Truth Social. Quelques minutes plus tard, Volodimir Zelensky a cependant indiqué ne pas avoir été informé d'une telle trêve, déclarant au site d'information Axios que l'annonce du président américain constituait "une surprise" pour lui. "L'Ukraine soutient le cessez-le-feu, et il est important que la Russie le soutienne également. Nous attendons des précisions de la partie américaine", a-t-il écrit par la suite sur l'application Telegram. "Pour sa part, l'Ukraine soutient toujours PLEINEMENT les mesures visant à la désescalade, à la protection des vies humaines et aux décisions nécessaires pour mettre fin à la guerre et garantir une paix durable." Moscou n'a pas commenté les annonces de Donald Trump dans l'immédiat. Plus tôt, Volodimir Zelensky s'était dit disposé à suspendre les attaques contre les raffineries de pétrole russes si Moscou cessait ses propres frappes contre les infrastructures énergétiques ukrainiennes, après que Donald Trump a exigé que Kyiv mette unilatéralement fin à ses assauts. Il a également déclaré qu'il organiserait des élections en Ukraine si le président russe Vladimir Poutine acceptait un cessez-le-feu global de 60 jours. Samedi, Donald Trump a imputé la hausse des prix du diesel aux États-Unis aux frappes ukrainiennes contre les raffineries russes et a déclaré que Volodimir Zelensky "ferait mieux d'arrêter immédiatement", ajoutant que l'Ukraine devrait le remplacer à sa tête car il avait laissé passer plusieurs occasions de conclure un accord avec Moscou. "DITES À POUTINE DE NOUS DONNER DEUX MOIS" La forte hausse des prix mondiaux du diesel, qui a suivi le déclenchement de la guerre avec l'Iran en février, est devenue un handicap politique pour le Parti républicain de Donald Trump à l'approche des élections de mi-mandat du mois prochain, lors desquelles les démocrates pourraient reprendre le contrôle d'une ou des deux chambres du Congrès. Volodimir Zelensky a réaffirmé dimanche la position de longue date de l'Ukraine, selon laquelle elle est disposée à cesser ses attaques contre les raffineries russes uniquement dans le cadre d'une désescalade réciproque du conflit, qui exigerait que Moscou mette également fin à ses frappes contre les infrastructures électriques ukrainiennes. Tout accord de ce type devrait s'accompagner de "garanties réelles", a déclaré Volodimir Zelensky. "La véritable cause de la guerre en Europe, c'est la Russie et la Russie seule", a-t-il dit, sans faire directement référence aux propos de Donald Trump. "Il est possible de mettre fin aux frappes contre les infrastructures énergétiques dès aujourd'hui, mais Vladimir Poutine ne le veut pas." "Dites à Poutine de nous donner deux mois, 60 jours de cessez-le-feu total, 60 jours, et nous organiserons des élections", a également déclaré Volodimir Zelensky à la chaîne américaine ABC. Samedi, il a réagi avec colère à l'annonce par Donald Trump d'un accord d'approvisionnement en diesel avec la Russie, estimant que celui-ci encouragerait les attaques de Moscou contre l'Ukraine. "UNE TRAHISON" Des analystes ont déclaré que l'accord conclu par Donald Trump avec Moscou avait peu de chances d'entraîner une baisse durable des prix des carburants, les volumes concernés restant bien inférieurs aux exportations habituelles de la Russie lorsque ses raffineries ne sont pas visées par des attaques. L'accord sur le diesel a également été critiqué par des élus américains, dont le représentant républicain Don Bacon, qui a estimé qu'il était temps de renforcer les sanctions plutôt que de les alléger. Dans les rues de Kyiv, plusieurs habitants ont fait part de leur colère après la suggestion de Donald Trump selon laquelle l'Ukraine devrait se trouver un nouveau dirigeant prêt à conclure un accord avec le président russe Vladimir Poutine. "Personne n'a le droit de nous dire ce que nous devons faire, d'autant que des élections ne peuvent pas être organisées en temps de guerre", a déclaré Sabina, une institutrice de 40 ans, en référence à l'interdiction des élections en Ukraine sous le régime de la loi martiale pour des raisons de sécurité. "À mes yeux, c'est une trahison de la part de nos partenaires", a-t-elle déclaré au sujet des remarques de Donald Trump. Volodimir Zelensky a déclaré qu'il poursuivrait dimanche ses discussions avec les dirigeants européens et que des échanges avaient lieu quotidiennement sur des dispositifs supplémentaires de défense aérienne, notamment des munitions pour les avions de combat utilisés pour abattre les drones russes à réaction. Lundi, le ministre ukrainien des Affaires étrangères, Andrii Sybiha, doit participer à une réunion du Conseil des affaires étrangères de l'Union européenne qui devrait examiner un renforcement de la pression des sanctions contre la Russie ainsi que l'avancement des négociations sur l'adhésion de l'Ukraine à l'Union européenne.

item.title: Trump announces Ukraine energy ceasefire with Russia, surprising Zelenskiy
item.description: There was no word from Moscow on the announcement, which followed days of intense pressure from Trump for Ukraine to halt its attacks on Russian oil refineries.
item.dc:creator: Daniel Flynn, Steve Holland
item.content:encoded: US President Donald Trump made a surprise announcement of an energy ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine on Sunday that he said was "effective immediately", but Ukrainian leader Volodymyr Zelenskiy said he was still waiting to see details of the deal. There was no word from Moscow on the announcement, which followed days of intense pressure from Trump for Ukraine to halt its attacks on Russian oil refineries. He blames those strikes for a rise in diesel prices that is hurting his Republican Party ahead of US midterm elections next month. In a dramatic deterioration in relations, Trump on Saturday warned Zelenskiy that he had [USN:L6N45W06G TEXT:""better damn well stop""] attacking Russian refineries, and urged Ukrainians to replace their leader at new elections. Trump said Zelenskiy had missed several opportunities to strike a deal with Moscow. In a post on his Truth Social platform on Sunday, Trump unexpectedly announced that Ukraine and Russia had agreed to an energy ceasefire, but did not elaborate further. "Effective immediately, there is an ENERGY CEASEFIRE in the War between Russia and Ukraine. Both parties have agreed. Do not break it!" Trump wrote. Trump, whose war in Iran has been widely blamed for hiking global fuel prices, had previously announced an energy ceasefire in Ukraine in [USN:FWN4560K2 TEXT:"mid-September"], although neither side ever confirmed such an agreement was reached. Zelenskiy said in a post on the Telegram app that he had discussed Trump's announcement with NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte, Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney and Finnish President Alexander Stubb. "Ukraine supports the ceasefire, and it is important that Russia support it as well. We are awaiting details from the American side," he said. Hours earlier, Zelenskiy had pushed back against US pressure for a unilateral end to Ukrainian attacks on Russian refineries, repeating his long-standing position that he was willing to do so only if President Vladimir Putin suspended Russian strikes on Ukrainian power infrastructure. Any such ceasefire agreement would need to come with "real guarantees", Zelenskiy said. "The real cause of the war in Europe is Russia and Russia alone," Zelenskiy said. "It's possible to stop strikes on energy infrastructure as early as today, but Putin does not want to do so." PROMISE OF ELECTIONS Trump also called for elections in Ukraine, suspended since the 2022 Russian invasion, to which Zelenskiy responded that he would call a vote if Putin agreed to a 60-day ceasefire. Zelenskiy said it was "up to Ukrainians" to choose their leader, but added that there needed to be an end to the fighting first. Ukrainian law [USN:L1N44G089 TEXT:"prohibits elections under martial law"] for security reasons. "Please tell Putin, give us two months, 60 days of total ceasefire, 60 days, and we will organise elections," Zelenskiy said. The Ukrainian leader rejected that he was to blame for energy price rises, adding that "everybody in the world" knew that the war in the Middle East was a bigger factor. The steep rise in global diesel prices, which followed the outbreak of the Iran war in February, has become a political liability for Trump's Republican Party ahead of the midterms, when opposition Democrats could gain control of one or both houses of Congress. On Saturday, Zelenskiy responded angrily to Trump's announcement of a diesel supply deal with Russia, saying it would embolden Moscow's attacks on Ukraine and lead to a greater loss of civilian lives. Analysts said Trump's diesel supply agreement with Moscow was unlikely to lead to sustained lower fuel prices as the volumes involved were too small. Under terms of the deal as described by Trump on Friday, Russia will immediately supply more than 300,000 metric tons of diesel to US and global markets, equal to about 2.25 million barrels of fuel. The US exports about 1.5 million barrels of diesel per day. The diesel deal was also criticized by US lawmakers, including one of Trump's fellow Republicans, Representative Don Bacon, who said it was time to apply more sanctions, not lift them. KYIV RESIDENTS ANGRY On the streets of Kyiv, several residents expressed anger at Trump's suggestion that Ukraine should find a new leader willing to make a deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin. "No one has the right to tell us what to do, especially since elections cannot be held during wartime," said Sabina, a 40-year-old primary school teacher. "In my view, it is a betrayal by our partners," she said, describing Trump's remarks. Zelenskiy said he would continue discussions with European leaders on Sunday, and there were daily conversations around additional air defence packages, including ammunition for combat aircraft that are used to down Russia's jet-powered drones. On Monday, Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha is due to participate in a European Union Foreign Affairs Council meeting that is expected to discuss increasing sanctions pressure on Russia and advancing negotiations on Ukraine's EU accession.

item.title: Gea sends Shelton crashing out of Shanghai
item.description: US Open finalist Ben Shelton conceded he had been "outplayed" after suffering a shock 7-6(5) 7-6(3) defeat by France's Arthur Gea in the third round of the Shanghai Masters on Sunday.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: US Open finalist Ben Shelton conceded he had been "outplayed" after suffering a shock 7-6(5) 7-6(3) defeat by France's Arthur Gea in the third round of the Shanghai Masters on Sunday. World number four Shelton, who has barely played since losing to Alexander Zverev in September's US Open final and withdrew from the Japan Open due to fitness concerns, lost both sets against the world number 56 in tight tiebreakers. Asked if his recent lack of action had had an effect on him, Shelton told reporters: "I mean, I got outplayed today. The guy played better than me. "A hundred percent, I would have liked to have come over here earlier and be prepared and have already dealt with the jet lag by the time I was playing here in the Shanghai Masters. "My body wasn't ready. I wasn't physically ready to play in Tokyo. That's just the way this tour is sometimes." The 24-year-old American said he was focused on finishing his 2026 campaign on a "high note" at the season-ending ATP Finals in Turin next month. "Obviously I want to be prepared and playing some of my best tennis when I get there," he added. "Three tournaments left to finish the year, which has been a very up and down year, but a great year, on a high note." Gea, who next faces either Jakub Mensik or Francisco Cerundolo, was delighted with his first win over a top-10 player. "I'm practicing hard every day since the beginning of the year to win against those guys," he said. "Of course, when you win, it is always special. But, yeah, I was prepared and I was confident before the match. Also playing a really good season right now, so, yeah, that's a really good win, but I was ready for it."

item.title: Hurricane Simon expected to become major hurricane off Mexico coast
item.description: Hurricane Simon is expected to become a major hurricane on Sunday near the west-central coast of Mexico and move very close to the coast on Monday, the US National Hurricane Center said.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: Hurricane Simon is expected to become a major hurricane on Sunday near the west-central coast of Mexico and move very close to the coast on Monday, the US National Hurricane Center said. Simon was located about 60 miles (96.56 km) west-southwest of Manzanillo, Mexico, early Sunday morning, packing maximum sustained winds of 155 mph, NHC said in its latest update.

item.title: L'aéroport de Ryad a encore été ciblé, dit la coalition dirigée par l'Arabie saoudite
item.description: La coalition dirigée par l'Arabie saoudite au Yémen a annoncé qu'un "projectile non identifié" avait frappé dimanche l'aéroport international de Ryad, provoquant un incendie, au lendemain d'une attaque contre ce même aéroport revendiquée par les Houthis qui a fait 12 morts.
item.dc:creator: Jana Choukeir, Maha Dahan, Timour Azhari
item.content:encoded: La coalition dirigée par l'Arabie saoudite au Yémen a annoncé qu'un "projectile non identifié" avait frappé dimanche l'aéroport international de Ryad, provoquant un incendie, au lendemain d'une attaque contre ce même aéroport revendiquée par les Houthis qui a fait 12 morts. Quelques heures auparavant, les Houthis avaient renouvelé leurs mises en garde contre l'utilisation des aéroports saoudiens, appelant les compagnies aériennes, les employés des aéroports et les voyageurs à s'en tenir éloignés. Le groupe soutenu par l'Iran a déclaré que les aéroports et l'espace aérien saoudiens demeuraient des cibles potentielles d'opérations militaires et a averti que le royaume porterait la responsabilité de toute interception qui échouerait. La coalition a également indiqué dimanche que les défenses aériennes saoudiennes avaient intercepté un missile de croisière à proximité de l'aéroport international du roi Khaled, sans plus de précisions. L'aéroport de la capitale saoudienne est resté fermé après l'attaque de samedi, qui a fait 12 morts et plus de 300 blessés, ce qui a constitué la frappe la plus meurtrière de ce type dans le royaume depuis plus d'une décennie, sur fond d'escalade des combats entre les Houthis et les forces gouvernementales yéménites. La coalition a précisé que l'engin tiré dimanche visait le terminal 4 de l'aéroport, sans fournir davantage d'explications. L'Arabie saoudite a intensifié ces dernières semaines son implication militaire au Yémen, menant des frappes contre les Houthis et soutenant une contre-offensive des forces gouvernementales après que le groupe s'est emparé le mois dernier de secteurs stratégiques le long de la côte de la mer Rouge. Le ministère yéménite des Affaires étrangères contrôlé par les Houthis a déclaré dimanche que toute nouvelle action militaire saoudienne au Yémen entraînerait une riposte de plus grande ampleur, ajoutant que ses actions seraient guidées par le principe de réciprocité. UN IMPORTANT CONGRÈS SUR L'ÉNERGIE MAINTENU À RYAD "Tant que l'ennemi saoudien ne mettra pas fin à son agression et à son ingérence au Yémen, le pire est à venir, si Dieu le veut", a déclaré le ministère dans des communiqués relayés par la chaîne Al Masirah, contrôlée par les Houthis. Le président Donald Trump a déclaré samedi que les États-Unis envisageaient de participer aux frappes saoudiennes contre les Houthis dans ce conflit, qui constitue une extension de la guerre contre l'Iran déclenchée en février par Washington et Israël. Ces nouvelles menaces interviennent alors que l'Arabie saoudite a maintenu l'accueil d'un important congrès international de l'énergie à Ryad. Le ministère saoudien de l'Énergie a annoncé que le 25e Congrès mondial de l'énergie (WPC Energy Congress), d'une durée de cinq jours, avait débuté dimanche avec la participation confirmée de plus de 70 ministres, 300 dirigeants d'entreprises et représentants de plus de 25 organisations internationales du secteur de l'énergie, selon la télévision d'État. La réunion ministérielle de l'International Energy Forum devait également se tenir dimanche, sa séance plénière étant organisée à huis clos, selon un avis aux médias. L'attaque de samedi a été la troisième visant l'aéroport de Ryad en une semaine. Parmi les victimes de celle-ci figurent quatre Saoudiens, deux Bangladais ainsi que des ressortissants des États-Unis, de Jordanie, de Palestine, de Syrie, du Soudan et d'Égypte.

item.title: INWIT investors line up financing for possible take-private, sources say
item.description: The leading shareholders in INWIT are arranging the financing for a potential take-private deal of Italy's largest mobile telecom towers company, two people close to the matter said, amid a contractual dispute between the masts firm and its two main customers.
item.dc:creator: Elvira Pollina, Amy-Jo Crowley, Valentina Za
item.content:encoded: The leading shareholders in INWIT (INWT.MI) are arranging the financing for a potential take-private deal of Italy's largest mobile telecom towers company, two people close to the matter said, amid a contractual dispute between the masts firm and its two main customers. French private equity firm Ardian and investment vehicle Oak Holdings 1, the latter backed by co-investors GIP, Vodafone (VOD.L) and KKR (KKR.N) , are exploring a bid to buy out minority shareholders in INWIT, the people said. Ardian controls 32% of INWIT, while Oak Holdings controls 39%. The investors are discussing the financing of the bid with banks, the people said, with one person adding that Abu Dhabi investment firm Mubadala is expected to take a stake in INWIT as part of the plan. The people cautioned that deliberations are still ongoing. Ardian, GIP, Vodafone (VOD.L) , KKR (KKR.N) and Mubadala declined to comment. GIP is part of US investment firm Blackrock (BLK.N) . An INWIT spokesperson said the company did not have any information on the matter. INWIT, which listed in Milan in 2015, has been the subject of [USN:L6N40C0Y4 TEXT:"takeover speculation"] since a French media report in February that infrastructure fund Ardian and investment group Brookfield were interested in taking the Italian company private. INWIT has since then become [USN:L8N43G1LQ TEXT:"embroiled in a dispute"] with its two main customers, Telecom Italia (TIM) (TLIT.MI) and Swisscom's Fastweb (SCMN.S) , both of which have initiated procedures to terminate their respective contracts with INWIT as part of efforts to renegotiate them on more favourable terms. INWIT's market value has fallen about 27% over the past year to $7.1 billion (€6.3 billion) as of Friday's close, according to LSEG data. (1 euro = $1.1201)

item.title: Polish police detain man after threat to PM
item.description: Polish police have detained a man suspected of planning an attack on Prime Minister Donald Tusk, the Interior Minister said on Sunday, after it warned earlier of a threat to Tusk and Defence Minister Wladyslaw Kosiniak-Kamysz.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: Polish police have detained a man suspected of planning an attack on Prime Minister Donald Tusk, the Interior Minister said on Sunday, after it warned earlier of a threat to Tusk and Defence Minister Wladyslaw Kosiniak-Kamysz. "The man who threatened and planned an attack on Prime Minister Donald Tusk has been detained by Polish police," Marcin Kierwinski wrote on X, without giving further details. Tusk thanked the police for "swift and decisive action" in a separate post on X. While violent crime is relatively rare in Poland, the country is deeply polarised politically and has faced security threats due to its proximity to the war in Ukraine. In August, police detained a 23-year-old man accused of [USN:L1N44I06W TEXT:"calling for the assassination"] of senior Polish politicians. In 2024, Tusk said he received threats after an [USN:L1N3W206N TEXT:"assassination attempt"] on Slovak Prime Minister Robert Fico. Interior Ministry Spokesperson Karolina Galecka said on Sunday an email with information about the potential attack had been forwarded to police by the State Protection Service, which is responsible for ministers' security.

item.title: From theatre to streets, Gen Z protester Neha Bora a new face of India's youth unrest
item.description: The 29-year-old doctoral student said she did not set out to become an activist.
item.dc:creator: Aftab Ahmed, Saurabh Sharma
item.content:encoded: A little-known doctoral student has emerged as one of the most visible faces of a protest movement in India that has mounted the most serious challenge to Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s government in years. Neha Bora, 29, is one of a number of prominent activists detained this weekend as the authorities cracked down on attempts by protesters led by the "Cockroach" youth movement to demonstrate against what they say is massive vote-rigging to help Modi's party. But Bora, national president of the left-wing All India Students’ Association, says she did not set out to become an activist. She traces her path into politics to theatre and, later, the student-led protests against a citizenship law in 2019 and 2020. BORA URGES PROTESTERS ON FROM DETENTION On Saturday, after police blocked demonstrators from reaching New Delhi's designated protest site, Jantar Mantar, Bora urged them to regroup at Dilli Haat, a crafts market 10 km (6 miles) away. "Dilli Haat becomes Jantar Mantar today," she wrote on X before setting off towards the site, chanting slogans as others followed. Police detained her with several other activists. But even in detention, she called for the demonstration to continue. "I am in detention. The movement is not," she said in a video posted online, urging supporters who were stopped by police to protest wherever they were. She was released later on Saturday. The Cockroach Janta Party-led protests seek the ouster of India's election chief, claiming irregularities in handling voter data have led to the deletion of 130 million names — more than the population of Japan — from electoral rolls. The Election Commission denies favouring any group, and Modi's Hindu nationalist party has accused opponents of trying to undermine the country's democracy by wrongly questioning legitimate electoral processes. Other issues Bora has championed include school-examination scandals, unemployment and police actions. Soft-spoken in conversation but forceful behind a microphone, she has built a following through speeches in Hindi and English, often invoking constitutional rights and linking student grievances to broader questions of inequality and government accountability. 'HOPE IS ALSO INFECTIOUS' Bora grew up in the Himalayan state of Uttarakhand and moved frequently as a child because her father served in the army. She studied at Delhi University before beginning a doctorate at Jawaharlal Nehru University's School of Arts and Aesthetics. As an undergraduate, she told Reuters in an interview this month, she joined a theatre group, where she learned to inhabit the lives of people much different from herself. "There might be a character that if you meet in your real life, you will disagree with, you will not like. But to do theatre is to understand where that person comes from." A turning point was the citizenship law, which critics say discriminates against Muslims. Bora said she watched students of her own generation lead classmates out of lecture halls and onto the streets, turning ideas she had encountered in books, films and documentaries into political action. She gained wider attention during protests in July over alleged leaks of exam papers, when she joined other activists in demanding the resignation of the education minister. Her speeches at Jantar Mantar, criticising the government and police response to demonstrators, circulated widely online. Bora has since become a fixture at demonstrations in the capital. During protests demanding the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar, she was repeatedly detained and returned to the streets after her release. She said ideology alone does not drive the current mobilisation, describing hope as a more powerful force. "Fear is infectious, of course. But hope is also infectious," she said. "People have courage now because they think that they can have courage." Bora said the demonstrations reflect the accumulation of years of grievances. "People remember," she said. "People carry that discontent, people carry that betrayal, people carry that disappointment."

item.title: Pakistan imposes emergency rule over Imran Khan's provincial government
item.description: Pakistan's president declared a state of emergency and suspended the provincial government of jailed former Prime Minister Imran Khan on Sunday, following allegations by the federal government that it has failed to tackle Islamist militancy.
item.dc:creator: Asif Shahzad, Ariba Shahid
item.content:encoded: Pakistan's president declared a state of emergency and suspended the provincial government of jailed former Prime Minister Imran Khan on Sunday, following allegations by the federal government that it has failed to tackle Islamist militancy. The constitution allows the federal government to take over some or all provincial government functions during an emergency. A provincial governor will take charge with an advisory council, Law Minister Azam Nazeer Tarar told a news conference in Islamabad, adding that the arrangement will initially be in place for six months. The interior ministry said it would be deploying troops in the northwestern Khyber Pakhtunkhwa province bordering Afghanistan, which has suffered an increasing number of [USN:L1N43Z03Y TEXT:"militant attacks"] in recent months. "The situation is so grave that you wouldn't see any residents coming out of their houses after evening in some of the districts," said Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi. The federal government and the military have accused Khan's party of failing to curb the militants, while Khan's party has rejected the accusation and says the federal government has failed to provide it with the funding and equipment needed. Islamabad accuses neighbouring Afghanistan of harboring Islamist militants who launch attacks inside Pakistan, and says that Khan's party had been sympathizing with both the Taliban in Kabul and their affiliates at home. Both the Afghan Taliban and Khan's party have denied the accusation. President Asif Ali Zardari declared an emergency on the advice of Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif following a federal cabinet decision, the president's office said. The security forces and citizens had been under attack for the last two years, Sharif told the Cabinet. "We can't just act a silent spectator." `COUP DISGUISED AS EMERGENCY` The move comes after Khan's Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf party rallied for several days to pressure the government for his release, threatening to [USN:L8N45R072 TEXT:"march on the capital"] Islamabad in coming days amid deepening political instability. Khan's supporters say the military rigged the 2024 election against the 74-year-old former cricket star, an allegation the military denies. "This is more of a coup disguised as emergency," said Zulfikar Bukhari, Khan's aide and his party's spokesperson, adding that it risks leading to further bloodshed and instability. Ahead of the planned march, authorities detained three of Khan's sisters and hundreds of party activists. Restrictions have been placed on the movements of Chief Minister, Sohail Afridi of Khan's party, one of his close aides told Reuters. The government has cut access to the capital, Islamabad, to bar the protesters from reaching parliament, blocking major highways with shipping containers and deploying tens of thousands of security forces, interior ministry officials said. The party's last large-scale protest two years ago ended in deadly clashes with security forces. Khan's 2023 arrest sparked nationwide riots that threatened the standing of the Pakistani military. Cases against Khan have ranged from concerns over state gifts to instigating violence and an accusation of an unlawful marriage. All convictions but one have since been suspended or overturned, with appeals pending. He denies wrongdoing. The latest protest coincides with public discontent over inflation and rising fuel prices that has spread beyond Khan's core supporters.

item.title: Bezzecchi pips Fernandez to win Indonesian GP, Martin retakes championship lead
item.description: Aprilia's Marco Bezzecchi ruthlessly hunted down injured Raul Fernandez to win the Indonesian Grand Prix on Sunday, while Jorge Martin came in third to retake the championship lead from rival Marc Marquez.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: Aprilia's Marco Bezzecchi ruthlessly hunted down injured Raul Fernandez to win the Indonesian Grand Prix on Sunday, while Jorge Martin came in third to retake the championship lead from rival Marc Marquez. [USN:L4N45W00O TEXT:"Polesitter Fernandez"], racing with fractured fingers sustained in a crash on Saturday, looked untroubled in the opening half of the race as he and Bezzecchi surged away from the chasing pack. But the Trackhouse rider began to fade as the afternoon wore on, and a determined Bezzecchi finally pounced with nine laps remaining to seize the lead and secure victory, with Martin completing a podium lockout for Italian manufacturer Aprilia. Bezzecchi's win, the 300th victory for an Italian in MotoGP, also kept his faint championship hopes alive. "I'm very, very happy to be back on the top step of the podium," said the 27-year-old, who led the standings in the early stages of the season but has struggled in recent weeks. "It was a nice, nice battle with Raul. I think we deserve a result like this, me and all my team, especially them, because they never stop working. They've been through tough times with me." A dejected Fernandez revealed the full extent of his injury after the race. "Yesterday, when I crashed and I saw my hand, I knew before going to the clinic that I had my finger broken, the one that normally I used to brake," the Spaniard said. "This morning, when I woke up, I realised I don't have one, but two fingers broken. No one knew. I tried to say nothing, just keep the pain for me and keep my focus on the race. "This morning, I tried find a solution on the brakes, because I was not able to use the finger that I use normally. I started everything from zero. It was a very difficult job for me." MARTIN BACK AT THE TOP The most exciting duel in the race took place behind the top three, with Marquez engaging in a thrilling back-and-forth with KTM's Pedro Acosta. Marquez had a strong start and swooped into third place in the opening lap, but his Ducati struggled to keep pace with the Aprilia machines around him, and a hard-charging Martin picked him off with ease in the third lap. The defending champion was then quickly overtaken by Acosta, but for the second time in as many days, Marquez profited from tyre pressure issues for his opponent and was allowed back into fourth. When Acosta was sure he would not receive a penalty, he once again locked horns with Marquez, but as they traded blows, Trackhouse's Ai Ogura capitalised and moved past both riders to seal a first-ever 1-2-3-4 finish for Aprilia. Martin, the 2024 champion, moved up to 355 points at the top of the championship standings, with [USN:L1N45W01V TEXT:"Saturday's sprint-winner Marquez"] on 353 points after finishing in sixth place - the first time he has completed a full race at the Mandalika circuit. "The last few laps, I was struggling a lot with the tyres, physical condition, but I was able to finish on the podium, so really, really happy," Martin said. "We are still in the fight. We are still in the lead. It will be a tough championship, but I will give my all."

item.title: Hurricanes aim to extend win streak to 5, add to Flyers' woes
item.description: Less than two weeks into the season, the Carolina Hurricanes and Philadelphia Flyers are heading in vastly different directions.
item.dc:creator: Field Level Media
item.content:encoded: Less than two weeks into the season, the Carolina Hurricanes and Philadelphia Flyers are heading in vastly different directions. The Hurricanes aim for their fifth straight victory Sunday when they visit the winless Flyers for the second consecutive weekend. Carolina lost its first two games before posting a 3-2 triumph in Philadelphia on Oct. 3. Former Flyer Shayne Gostisbehere scored the overtime winner for the Hurricanes, who used that victory as a springboard to three more wins. Most recently, Carolina posted a 5-2 road victory over the Chicago Blackhawks on Saturday. Jackson Blake and Jordan Martinook each registered a goal and an assist for the Hurricanes. "Every single line is contributing," Martinook said. "The 'D' is playing some of the best hockey I've ever seen the group play together. ... It's been fun to watch." Sebastian Aho added a shorthanded goal for his team-leading fifth goal, while Mark Jankowski and Taylor Hall also scored for the defending Stanley Cup champions. "We've definitely, after the first couple games, gotten into our game," Aho said. "Just playing Hurricanes hockey, and that usually gives you a chance to win." The Hurricanes have scored 21 goals during their four-game winning streak. Jankowski has scored in each of the last three games, while Brandon Bussi has earned the victory in each of his last two starts. "It was a good effort from pretty much everyone," Carolina coach Rod Brind'Amour said. "I liked it. ... When we're going, you can tell we're in sync." Philadelphia, meanwhile, has lost 10 straight games dating back to its second-round playoff series against Carolina. The Hurricanes swept the Flyers last spring en route to winning the Stanley Cup, and the hangover has continued into the current campaign, as Philadelphia is 0-4-2. "It's not like we're not trying," said rookie forward Porter Martone, who scored the Flyers' goal in Saturday's 5-1 road loss to the Boston Bruins. "These guys in this group, we care. I think a lot of people from the outside think it's lack of effort, but everyone in this room is giving it their all. We don't like this. We're not having fun right now. We want to win." Philadelphia has been outshot by a wide margin and outscored 24-7 in its first six games. The Flyers scored only three goals while going 0-2-1 on their three-game road trip that ended Saturday. The last time the Flyers lost their first six games was in 2008-09, when the team began 0-3-3 before rallying to make the postseason. "You've got to stick together," said Philadelphia coach Rick Tocchet, whose team played Saturday without forward Travis Konecny and defensemen Rasmus Ristolainen and Cam York. "We're at the bottom. We're in the muck right now. Hopefully, we get some healthy bodies back, but you've just got to stick together. There's no other answer. We've all been, in life, in a situation where you're in a foxhole and we need some people to sit in a foxhole and stick together." --Field Level Media

item.title: Most Gulf stocks in red after attack on Riyadh airport
item.description: Most Gulf stock markets ended lower on Sunday, as geopolitical concerns weighed on sentiment after an attack on Riyadh's international airport left at least 12 dead and more than 300 wounded, marking the kingdom's deadliest attack in over a decade.
item.dc:creator: Ateeq Shariff
item.content:encoded: Most Gulf stock markets ended lower on Sunday, as geopolitical concerns weighed on sentiment after an [USN:L1N45W03M TEXT:"attack on Riyadh's international airport"] left at least 12 dead and more than 300 wounded, marking the kingdom's deadliest attack in over a decade. Adding to the uncertainty, Yemen's Houthis on Sunday [USN:L1N45X01E TEXT:"warned airlines, travellers and airport workers to stay away from Saudi airports"]. Saudi Arabia's benchmark index (.TASI) narrowed early losses to finish 0.2% lower with the country's biggest lender by assets Saudi National Bank (1180.SE) losing 1.1%. Oil major Saudi Aramco (2222.SE) was down 0.2%. President Donald Trump has said Washington was considering joining Saudi strikes against the Iran-backed Houthis, widening a regional conflict that spilled over from the US-Israeli war with Iran. Riyadh and the Saudi-backed Yemeni government have claimed hundreds of strikes against targets in Houthi-held territory in Yemen. The Houthis have said these killed civilians including women and children. Reuters could not independently verify those claims. In Qatar, the benchmark index (.QSI) declined 1.5%, falling for a fourth consecutive session and closing at its lowest since May 2020, with Qatar Islamic Bank (QISB.QA) declining 1.7%. Geopolitical risks continue to weigh on sentiment, with stalled US-Iran talks constraining risk appetite and reports of renewed escalation adding to caution. Concerns are likely to remain elevated as tanker attacks and maritime disruptions in the Strait of Hormuz persist, said Milad Azar, market analyst at XTB MENA. Outside the Gulf, Egypt's blue-chip index (.EGX30) - which traded after a session's break — declined 2%, with all its constituents closing in negative territory including Commercial International Bank (COMI.CA) , which was down 1.6%. Saudi Arabia (.TASI) lost 0.2% to 10,361 Qatar (.QS) dropped 1.5% to 8,875 Egypt (.EGX30) declined 2% to 52,207 Bahrain (.BAX) fell 0.3% to 1,890 Oman (.MSX30) added 0.3% to 7,842 Kuwait (.BKP) inched 0.1% higher to 9,037

item.title: Rangers begin life without Igor Shesterkin vs. slumping Canucks
item.description: The New York Rangers were bracing for the worst when Igor Shesterkin's right skate crashed into the goal post Friday night.
item.dc:creator: Field Level Media
item.content:encoded: The New York Rangers were bracing for the worst when Igor Shesterkin's right skate crashed into the goal post Friday night. On Saturday, the Rangers found out Shesterkin's season was over, and his absence threatens to derail a promising start for a team coming off missing the playoffs for the past two seasons. Dylan Garand will step in as the 2021-22 Vezina Trophy winner's replacement for the time being, and the Rangers hope his promise in limited action translates to success in regular work starting Sunday night when they host the Vancouver Canucks. Shesterkin, 30, was injured when his right skate collided with the goal post while sliding into position to make a save with 11:40 remaining in the second period of Friday's 3-1 loss at Washington, which halted a four-game winning streak. Shesterkin's season is over after he was 3-1-0 with a 1.79 goals-against average. The Rangers are now counting on Garand, who is 3-1-1 with a 1.31 GAA in five career games. "You never want to see guys get injured, especially your best player in Igor," Garand, 24, told reporters at practice Saturday. "He means a lot to the guys in this room and a lot to me personally. ... I'm excited for the opportunity. Going to put my heart and soul on the line for these guys and this city every night and just try to help the team win." Garand began this season third on New York's depth chart and was exposed to waivers before getting claimed. He is being elevated because Joonas Korpisalo is out for at least four more weeks due to a lower-body injury. Garand's backup will be journeyman Spencer Martin, who made six appearances last season when Shesterkin was injured in January and went 1-3-0 with a 4.13 GAA. "A guy (Shesterkin) that means so much to our team," defenseman Adam Fox told reporters at practice Saturday. "Obviously, still processing that and you still feel terrible. Personally having dealt with injuries the past few years and him, too, it (stinks) when you're not able to be out there and help the team. He's such an important piece to this team. It's an opportunity for everyone else to step up." The Rangers are hoping Garand can help them open a season 4-0 at home for the first time since 2009-10 after outscoring Tampa Bay, Utah and the Islanders 14-5. Vancouver has allowed a league-leading 29 goals through its first six games, including 14 in a three-game skid against the Vegas Golden Knights, Carolina Hurricanes and New Jersey Devils. The Canucks have permitted 98 shots on goal in their past three games, and have allowed three power-play goals apiece in the past two games. "From a work ethic standpoint, it just needs to be much more difficult for teams to recover pucks and get to their sets," first-year coach Manny Malhotra said of Vancouver's penalty-killing woes. Last season, the Canucks had the NHL's worst penalty-kill percentage at 71.5%. "That's a couple games in a row where our penalty kill has to bear down and get those kills," Vancouver forward Brock Boeser said after taking a pair of penalties against the Devils. "We got to stay out of the box, myself included." --Field Level Media

item.title: Russia's Yandex says data centre in Vladimir area shut down after drone attack
item.description: Russian technology and AI company Yandex said on Sunday that its infrastructure had been damaged in a drone attack, resulting in the complete shutdown of its data centre in the Vladimir region.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: Russian technology and AI company Yandex said on Sunday that its infrastructure had been damaged in a drone attack, resulting in the complete shutdown of its data centre in the Vladimir region. No one was injured in the attack, but some of Yandex's services are currently unavailable to users, the company said. This is the third major data centre to have been taken out of action in the last few days. On Friday, Yandex, which is heavily involved in Russia's AI development and is sometimes called "Russia's Google", [USN:R4N45F01R TEXT:"said"] its data centre in the Kaluga region southwest of Moscow had been struck by Ukrainian drones and partly put out of action. A day earlier, a Ukrainian attack [USN:L1N45U04H TEXT:"shut down"] Yandex's data hub in Sasovo, southeast of Moscow, where two of the three supercomputers used to develop the company's AI model are housed.
