item.title: Protesters seeking India election chief's ouster detained, as 'cockroach' leaders released
item.description: Youth protesters, many of them from student organizations affiliated with India's communist parties, launched sporadic protests around the city on Sunday afternoon before police hauled them away in vehicles.
item.dc:creator: Saurabh Sharma, Sarita Singh, Arpan Chaturvedi, Shilpa Jamkhandikar
item.content:encoded: Police detained hundreds of protesters in Delhi for a second day on Sunday as sporadic protests broke out demanding India's election chief quit, while a court ordered the release of "cockroach" movement founder [USN:L1N45W01X TEXT:"Abhijeet Dipke"] and two other senior leaders. Dipke and the other leaders of the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP), a nationwide youth protest movement, were [USN:L1N45W00K TEXT:"detained"] when their plane landed in Delhi on Saturday as the movement planned to gather thousands of people at Jantar Mantar in Central Delhi. The court ordered their release with an undertaking to "maintain public peace", the CJP said in a statement. The youth movement, which has mobilised protests in recent months against a range of issues from government school infrastructure to jobs for young people, is one of the biggest political challenges to Prime Minister Narendra Modi and his Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) in his 12 years in power. The protesters are calling for the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner [USN:L4N45K0DB TEXT:"Gyanesh Kumar"] over a [USN:L1N45V037 TEXT:"revision of voter lists"] that critics say disproportionately benefits Modi. NEW PROTESTS IN DELHI, OTHER CITIES Youth protesters, many of them from students organisations affiliated with India's communist parties, launched sporadic protests on Sunday afternoon in Delhi before police detained them and hauled them away in vehicles. Small protests by dozens of people were also held in the cities of Mumbai, Kolkata, Panaji and Pune, local media reported. Abhita Ruheja, a protester who was detained on Sunday, said the authorities had turned Delhi into a fortress. "Is this how a democracy works? They have been scrapping rights after rights and this is turning into a dictatorship," she said. The All India Students' Association alleged in a post on X that those detained in Delhi were assaulted by police inside the vehicles. A video posted on X by the Communist Party of India (Marxist) showed one of its lawmakers, John Brittas, who was briefly detained, being helped from a bus to an autorickshaw as he appeared to be in distress. Reuters could not verify claims about detainees being assaulted by police. WE WILL HIT THE STREETS AGAIN, DIPKE SAYS Police also detained several journalists covering the protests, many of whom were carrying microphones and had their press cards prominently displayed, according to a Reuters witness. A Delhi Police spokesperson did not respond at a media briefing to questions about the alleged assaults and detentions. CJP's Dipke said he was going back to his home in India's western state of Maharashtra as his grandmother had died but added that the protests would continue. "Haven’t signed any bond that says we won’t protest. We will hit the streets again," he said in a post on X. Thousands of police and paramilitary personnel continued to be deployed across Delhi, although metro stations reopened and mobile internet services were restored after authorities locked down the city in an attempt to thwart Saturday's protests. The police spokesperson said 2,400 people were detained on Saturday and most were released the same night. Opposition parties and critics of Modi's government criticised what they said was the high-handed use of force against the protesters, while a UN body called on authorities to ensure that the right to peaceful assembly was respected and fulfilled. India's foreign ministry said the UN's statement constituted "an unwarranted interference in the internal affairs of India". POLL PANEL, BJP DENY MANIPULATION ALLEGATIONS At an unusually packed hearing on a Sunday, the Supreme Court recorded the government's assurance that lawyers and journalists would not be impeded while performing their duties. Lawyers protesting outside the Supreme Court were detained briefly on Saturday, as were several reporters including a Reuters journalist. Sporadic protests have been going on across India since the Indian Express newspaper in late September reported that Kumar's two deputies had raised several concerns internally about voter list revisions, registration procedures and digital systems. The Election Commission says differing views are normal in internal deliberations, and has denied favouring any party. Election Commission data shows about 130 million names, more than the population of Japan, have been deleted from electoral rolls during the verification exercise, including 28 million people who had died, 63 million who had relocated and 30 million who could not be traced. Modi's BJP has accused groups opposed to it of trying to undermine the country's democracy by wrongly questioning legitimate electoral processes. The Election Commission has said that voters wrongly deleted can re-enrol. The BJP and the Commission deny allegations of manipulation, although opposition parties allege Muslim voters and other minorities, who are unlikely to support the Hindu nationalist ruling party, are disproportionately impacted by the deletions.

item.title: Middle East war, high debt levels to dominate IMF-World Bank meetings in Bangkok
item.description: Finance officials from around the world will gather in Bangkok this week under the shadow of a widening war in the Middle East, the biggest-ever energy supply shock and rising interest rates that together pose daunting risks to already-sluggish global economic growth.
item.dc:creator: Andrea Shalal
item.content:encoded: Finance officials from around the world will gather in Bangkok this week under the shadow of a widening war in the Middle East, the biggest-ever energy supply shock and rising interest rates that together pose daunting risks to already-sluggish global economic growth. The US-Israeli-led war with Iran, now in its eighth month, and its inflationary impact, will dominate the agenda and sideline conversations during the annual meetings of the International Monetary Fund and World Bank, being held outside of Washington for the first time in three years. IMF Managing Director Kristalina Georgieva told Reuters during a tour of the 300,000 square-meter Queen Sirikit National Convention Center on Sunday evening that 18,000 people were registered to attend the meetings, 4,000 more than the last off-site meetings held in Morocco in October 2023. SEVERAL FINANCE MINISTERS STAYING AWAY Notably absent will be [USN:L1N45V0KM TEXT:"US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent"], who dispatched two senior officials in his stead while he handles some "domestic engagements," a US official said. Federal Reserve Board Chairman Kevin Warsh will attend and is slated to participate in a public event with Georgieva on October 16. Several other finance ministers were also staying home due to domestic budget and election duties, but most central bankers would attend, Georgieva said. Bessent's decision to skip the high-profile gathering and a meeting of the Group of 20 major economies, which the U.S. leads this year, may frustrate counterparts amid rising tensions over the Iran war, Ukraine's battle against Russia's invasion and the U.S. move to impose sanctions on the [USN:L8N45U28I TEXT:"International Criminal Court"]. World Bank President Ajay Banga told Reuters that while global growth had held up better than feared when Iran closed the Strait of Hormuz, shutting off some 20% of the world's oil, pressures were building again. Soaring prices for diesel, rising fertilizer prices and a looming [USN:L6N44V0FF TEXT:""super" El Niño weather effect"] that experts say could lead to 450,000 heat-related deaths are all hitting at once. RELEASE OF RESERVES Group of Seven countries have agreed to [USN:B5N44301Y TEXT:"release 100 million barrels of diesel"] and crude oil from emergency reserves under pressure from U.S. President Donald Trump, who is keen to see lower gasoline prices before November elections that could see his Republican Party lose control of Congress. Trump on Friday announced a deal with Russia that would provide even more diesel to global markets and a temporary waiver of [USN:S0N43U024 TEXT:"U.S. sanctions"] designed to deprive Moscow of revenues for its war on Ukraine. The move drew swift criticism from Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy. More than 1 billion barrels of oil have been released mainly from onshore commercial inventories since the start of the war on February 28, but industry executives say the [USN:L6N45S103 TEXT:"amount of oil in storage"] that is accessible to the global market is running low, making the market more fragile and fueling pressure on prices. Banga said the Bank was not revising down its global forecasts at the moment, but was keeping a close eye on developments. "The real thing is not just El Niño by itself; it's the combination ... What's happening to fertilizer prices? What's happening to energy costs? What's happening to debt? It's that put together that creates its own challenges," he said. "And I think that will call upon all of us to be far more careful on what we prepare for in the coming months." RISING DEBT IMF chief [USN:L1N45S0Z3 TEXT:"Georgieva"] issued a similar warning in her traditional curtain-raiser speech previewing the meetings last week, telling the audience: "Winter is coming." The IMF has signaled little change in its forecast for 3% global growth in 2026 and may edge its forecast for next year slightly higher. But some countries will see downgrades, including Ukraine, now in its fifth year of war against Russia's invasion, and Gulf countries hit by Iranian strikes and sharply reduced energy exports. IMF research released on Tuesday showed that [USN:L1N45R02Q TEXT:"sharp spikes in food and energy prices"] are an increasingly common source of crises that drive inflation expectations higher for longer, worsen poverty and threaten economic stability. One huge headache for policymakers is the growing public debt burden that is sapping growth and adding inflationary pressures. The IMF says public debt is at the highest level since World War Two and will exceed 100% of GDP before 2030. Advanced economies, led by the United States, have the highest debt-to-GDP ratios, but emerging markets and low-income countries are particularly vulnerable, given a perfect storm of challenges: capital outflows in search of higher US rates, El Niño, and lack of investment in AI, which has mitigated negative supply shocks in the US and other rich countries. EMERGING MARKET CONCERNS Developing countries are particularly vulnerable given high public debt levels that will have to be renegotiated at higher interest rates. Together, they face $400 billion in debt payments to external creditors in 2026, and interest payments already exceed 10% of revenue on average. Early in the COVID crisis, G20 leaders announced a suspension of debt service payments for the poorest countries, but there is little appetite for such action now, according to diplomats from G20 countries, who said high debt levels and political pressures posed bigger hurdles this time. Many lower-income countries are worried about new IMF recommendations for loan programs that call for fewer, but deeper reforms as a condition for approving lending, a change that many fear will lead to painful austerity measures. "Countries are already cutting their expenditures because their debt payments are going high and because of the IMF conditionality," said Iolanda Fresnillo, who works on debt justice for Eurodad. "We fear that this review of conditionality policy is just going to make things worse." Kenya, she said, had avoided a debt restructuring by cutting public expenditures and trying to raise taxes, but the changes sparked significant protests, especially by the young. The IMF risked losing credibility unless it acknowledged the severity of the crisis facing many developing countries. "As long as they continue with the governance structure that they have, they are becoming less and less relevant," she said. SECURITY AND FINANCE Flight routes to Bangkok often route through the Middle East, posing immediate security challenges to global travelers descending on Thailand's bustling capital city of 9 million residents following recent [USN:L1N45W03M TEXT:"attacks on Saudi airports"]. The last off-site annual meetings of the IMF and World Bank took place in Morocco just days after militants led by [USN:L8N45S0ZS TEXT:"Hamas killed 1,200 people in Israel"], followed by Israel's bombardment of Gaza that killed more than 74,000 people and devastated cities throughout the Palestinian area. Three years later, the linkage between national security and international finance is clear, although finance officials at the time had dismissed the Hamas attack as not being an economic issue, said Josh Lipsky, vice president of international economics at the Atlantic Council. "Obviously there have been massive global ramifications," he said. "What we're currently experiencing with Iran and the closure of the Strait of Hormuz has a direct connection with what happened three years ago." Policymakers needed to become more agile in responding to geopolitical crises in an increasingly interconnected world, Lipsky said. "They have to be proactive and they have to recognize that they don't live in the world they used to."

item.title: Nepal urges villagers to evacuate after flood triggered by landslide, 5 missing
item.description: Nepali authorities urged villagers on Sunday to move to safer places after a flood in a river in the central part of the country swept away several houses and infrastructure, but there were no reports of any casualties.
item.dc:creator: Gopal Sharma
item.content:encoded: Nepali authorities urged villagers on Sunday to move to safer places after a flood in a river in the central part of the country swept away several houses and infrastructure, but there were no reports of any casualties. Two women and three men were out of contact, the national disaster authority said. The army said a further 49 people, including a foreigner, had been rescued. They did not give the person's nationality. A landslide in Chumnubri village in Gorkha district, about 100 km (62 miles) west of Kathmandu, blocked the Budhi Gandaki River, leading to downstream flooding, authorities said. The Budhi Gandaki is a tributary of the Trishuli River, downstream from another tributary where a glacier collapse caused a catastrophic flood in August that killed 1,457 people, with thousands still missing. "We have asked villagers living along the river banks downstream to evacuate and remain safe," said Dharmendra Kumar Mishra, the Gorkha district's most senior bureaucrat. The flood swept away about a dozen houses and two suspension bridges and damaged a hydroelectric project camp, carrying some of the construction equipment away, the National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority said. The flooded river carrying muddy sludge was rising and had washed away a highway bridge connecting Gorkha with the neighbouring Dhading district, said Dharam Raj Uprety, chief of the Authority. National disaster authorities alerted people living along the river in the Gorkha, Tanahun, Chitwan, East Nawalparasi and West Nawalparasi districts about the flood. "Please help ensure that people in at-risk areas are moved to safe locations in time and assist search and rescue operations as needed," the National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority said in a social media post. Officials said army and police rescue personnel had reached the area and were also monitoring the situation from a helicopter.

item.title: Justice Department probes TV networks over Trump pool boycott
item.description: The US Justice Department said on Saturday it is investigating whether television networks violated federal antitrust laws over their decision to boycott covering the White House following its decision to pull the credentials of reporters from three news organizations, including CNN.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: The US Justice Department said on Saturday it is investigating whether television networks violated federal antitrust laws over their decision to boycott covering the White House following its decision to pull the credentials of reporters from three news organizations, including CNN. The networks under investigation are ABC, CBS, CNN, NBC and Fox News, the Justice Department said. "Group boycotts among commercial competitors can violate the Sherman Act," a Justice Department spokesperson said. "The Antitrust Division is simply investigating to determine whether these news organizations have violated the antitrust laws." The investigation is the latest in a series of clashes between the Trump administration and major news organizations. President Donald Trump has repeatedly called the mainstream media "fake news" and frequently clashes with reporters during encounters with the press. The action also puts legal and potentially financial pressure on the media to continue coverage of the president even when they disagree with how the White House handles them. The networks did not immediately respond to requests from Reuters for comment. The New York Times was first to report about the probe. The investigation comes after weeks of tension between the White House and the press. CREDENTIALS REVOKED IN SEPTEMBER On September 19, the White House blocked reporters from CNN, Politico, and MS NOW from entering the building, revoking their credentials. The White House said covering the president was a "privilege – not a right.” The outlets sued the administration, alleging the exclusions violated the First Amendment and that the White House was retaliating over their coverage. CNN is one of the five news organizations — along with ABC, CBS, Fox News and NBC — that make up the primary White House television pool. They share the costs of covering the president, take turns organizing coverage and share the footage with outlets around the country. All of the five television networks that cover the White House, including Fox News, suspended coverage in solidarity and refused to provide replacement coverage. The White House reinstated the credentials on September 24 after US District Judge Timothy Kelly ruled that the ban was likely unconstitutional and ordered the administration to "immediately return, reinstate, and restore" their access. However, disputes over access to specific presidential events and pool assignments continued afterward.

item.title: Nico Hischier scores milestone goal, leads Devils past Canucks
item.description: Nico Hischier scored twice on the power play, including his 200th career goal, and the New Jersey Devils rallied to beat the Vancouver Canucks 4-1 on Saturday afternoon in Newark, N.J.
item.dc:creator: Field Level Media
item.content:encoded: Nico Hischier scored twice on the power play, including his 200th career goal, and the New Jersey Devils rallied to beat the Vancouver Canucks 4-1 on Saturday afternoon in Newark, N.J. Jake Allen made 20 saves in his 500th career game to get the win as New Jersey snapped a two-game losing skid. Jesper Bratt had a goal and an assist, Jesper Boqvist also scored and Jack Hughes had two assists for the Devils, who finished with three goals on the power play to claim their second win of the season. Hischier, who signed a five-year, $58.5 million deal in the offseason, also had an assist. Linus Karlsson had a goal while Leevi Merilainen and Kevin Lankinen combined to stop 33 shots for the Canucks, who suffered their third consecutive loss. Paul Cotter, the NHL's Third Star of the Week, was held pointless in his first game with the Canucks against his former team. The teams traded power-play goals to open the scoring in the first period. Karlsson gave the Canucks a 1-0 lead with a power play goal on a one-timer after taking a pass from Brock Boeser. Hischier busted out of an early slump to score his first point of the season and 200th goal to tie it 1-1 with Vancouver forward Jonathan Lekkerimaki off for high-sticking. The Devils then recorded their first regulation lead of the season by capitalizing on a Canucks miscue in the Vancouver zone. Amadeus Lombardi stole the puck from Canucks defenseman Filip Hronek, then took a shot that generated a rebound which was poked in by forward Boqvist to make it 2-1 at 16:24 of the first period. Boqvist's goal came against Lankinen, who entered the game after starter Merilainen sustained an equipment malfunction when his skate blade fell out. Merilainen left the game with 5:27 remaining in the first and returned for the start of the second period. Bratt took advantage of a mad scramble in the Canucks' crease early in the second, scoring on the power play from a sharp angle with a shot that ricocheted off a couple Vancouver players into the net to give the Devils a two-goal lead. Hischier finished off a tic-tac-toe passing play for his second power play goal with just 10 seconds left in the second to make it 4-1. --Field Level Media

item.title: Bruins score 3 goals in final period, keep Flyers winless
item.description: Capping a three-point effort, Fraser Minten's second goal of the season concluded a three-goal third period for the Boston Bruins in a 5-1 win over the visiting Philadelphia Flyers on Saturday afternoon.
item.dc:creator: Field Level Media
item.content:encoded: Capping a three-point effort, Fraser Minten's second goal of the season concluded a three-goal third period for the Boston Bruins in a 5-1 win over the visiting Philadelphia Flyers on Saturday afternoon. Pavel Zacha and Mason Lohrei scored to give Boston leads after the first two periods before the emphatic finish. Marat Khusnutdinov and Casey Mittelstadt also lit the lamp, while Minten and JJ Peterka each had two assists. Jeremy Swayman made 14 saves en route to the Bruins' second straight win and fourth through their first six games. Boston finished with a 32-15 shots on goal advantage. Porter Martone scored a power-play goal and Dan Vladar (27 saves) took the loss for Philadelphia, which remains winless at 0-4-2 on the season. The Flyers were missing forward Travis Konecny (lower-body) and defenseman Cam York (upper-body) due to day-to-day injuries. Zacha's first goal of the season at the 12:24 mark punctuated a dominant opening period in which Boston held a 12-3 edge in shots, including holding Philadelphia without a chance during its first power play. Less than one minute after the Bruins completed a solid kill, David Pastrnak moved into the zone off a turnover at the blue line and dropped a backhand pass for Zacha, whose shot from the high slot leaked through Vladar and dribbled over the goal line for the opening tally. The visitors went without a shot for more than half of the second period, but Swayman stood up to the task of Martone's driving backhander with 9:51 to go. Lohrei doubled Boston's lead with 2:48 left in the middle frame. After Swayman's save on a David Jiricek point shot created an odd-man rush, Minten started the play and Peterka fed the trailing defenseman for a top-shelf wrister coming to the top of the circles. The Bruins needed only 1:55 of third-period time to make it a 3-0 game, as Khusnutdinov slammed home Minten's pass from behind the net following a crisp sequence between the duo and defenseman Will Borgen. Martone broke the shutout at 6:32, placing a tight-angle wrister from the left circle upstairs on Swayman. At 9:21, Boston regained its three-goal advantage after Casey Mittelstadt joined Lohrei with his second goal in as many games. After James Hagens had an initial shot saved by Vladar, he made a diagonal pass to Elias Lindholm in the bottom of the right circle, and Mittelstadt buried it in front. Minten put the exclamation point on the victory with 4:01 to go, speeding past a defender and down the left side to slip a quick shot five-hole on Vladar. --Field Level Media

item.title: Hurricane Simon strengthens to Category 4 off Mexico coast
item.description: Simon is forecast to be near or just inland of Mexico's west-central Pacific coast on Sunday.
item.dc:creator: Daniel Becerril, Alberto Fajardo
item.content:encoded: Hurricane Simon strengthened into a powerful Category 4 storm off Mexico's Pacific coast on Saturday, threatening destructive winds, storm surges and potentially deadly flooding as it approaches landfall. The US National Hurricane Center said Simon was located about 115 miles (185 km) south-southwest of Manzanillo, Mexico, on Saturday morning, packing maximum sustained winds of 150 mph (240 kph) as it moved northward. Simon is expected to approach the west-central coast of Mexico as a major hurricane late on Saturday or early Sunday, and some additional strengthening remains possible before landfall, the NHC said. A hurricane warning was in effect for portions of Mexico's Pacific coast south of the beach resort of Puerto Vallarta, including the area around Manzanillo, Mexico's largest Pacific port. A tropical storm watch was in effect farther south toward Lazaro Cardenas. The NHC urged residents in the warning area, which also includes the Islas Marias archipelago offshore, to rush preparations to protect life and property. “Simon has strengthened incredibly quickly, and that’s what makes storms like this so dangerous,” said AccuWeather meteorologist Dan Pydynowski. “Strong winds could damage homes and businesses, while flooding and mudslides could wash out roads and make it difficult for emergency crews to reach some communities. Even after the storm passes, power outages and damaged infrastructure could make recovery challenging.” PREPARATIONS UNDER WAY IN MANZANILLO In the early afternoon on Saturday in Manzanillo, residents appeared largely calm despite the approaching storm, with little sign of panic buying at supermarkets, according to a Reuters reporter on the ground. Some stores had begun boarding up their windows, while businesses were closing and streets were relatively empty. Rain had been falling intermittently since late on Friday, and rising seas were pushing waves almost to the entrances of beachfront hotels, although strong winds had yet to arrive. Civil protection workers had closed beaches, erected barriers and raised red and black warning flags, urging residents to stay away from the shore. Marines, soldiers, National Guard officers and emergency personnel were patrolling areas vulnerable to flooding and landslides, while authorities had begun precautionary evacuations in parts of Cihuatlan, a flood-prone municipality in neighboring Jalisco state, near Manzanillo. Rivers in some areas were already running high, raising concerns they could overflow if heavy rains intensified. Mexican authorities warned that heavy rainfall was expected in the states of Guerrero, Michoacan, Colima and Jalisco. UP TO 30 INCHES OF RAIN EXPECTED The NHC said Simon was expected to produce 10 to 20 inches (25 to 51 cm) of rain across portions of southwestern Mexico through Sunday, with isolated totals of up to 30 inches (76 cm) possible in parts of Michoacan, Colima and Jalisco. The rainfall could trigger life-threatening flooding and mudslides, especially in mountainous areas. A storm surge is expected along the coast near and to the east of where the center makes landfall, accompanied by large and destructive waves, the NHC said. Swells generated by Simon are expected to affect portions of Mexico's southwestern and west-central coast over the coming days, creating dangerous surf and rip current conditions. Simon is forecast to be near or just inland of Mexico's west-central Pacific coast on Sunday. Last week, Hurricane Polo made landfall on the Baja California Peninsula as a Category 2 storm, toppling trees and utility poles, flooding streets and causing other property damage.

item.title: UN Human Rights office condemns racist abuse targeting Gauff
item.description: The United Nations Human Rights office has condemned online racist abuse faced by Coco Gauff after a replayed point sparked a backlash against the American tennis player this week.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: The United Nations Human Rights office has condemned online racist abuse faced by Coco Gauff after a replayed point [USN:L4N45S06O TEXT:"sparked a backlash"] against the American tennis player this week. Gauff was targeted after stopping play during a crucial point in her win over Sun Xinran at the China Open, raising her hand to complain about a flickering advertising board as Sun was about to hit a winner. Women's tennis governing body WTA responded to the incident, saying they were appalled by the racist abuse directed at Gauff, and are in contact with her to offer full support. "As we do for all WTA players experiencing online abuse, our Threat Matrix team is monitoring the abusive messages, working with the athlete’s team to report them to the relevant platforms and seeking action on the content and the accounts responsible," WTA told Reuters in a statement. The umpire ordered the point to be replayed after a video review, and Gauff went on to win the match 7-5 6-1, but the American later revealed in a social media post that she had received a huge amount of racist abuse following the match. "You can dislike me or disagree about what happened without being racist," Gauff, who is Black, said on X in reply to a post containing a racial slur. The official UN Human Rights office posted a statement on Saturday calling for players, coaches and sports bodies to unite against racial and sexist abuse. "Racist messages such as those targeting tennis player Coco Gauff online are appalling and illustrate that Black female athletes are specifically targeted for vitriol and racial abuse," it wrote on X. "There is no place in sport for racial or sexist slurs and abuse. Players, coaches, and sports bodies need to stand up for those facing such attacks and fans need to push back against those who sully sport with racism and sexism." Two-time Grand Slam winner Gauff [USN:L1N45T0DY TEXT:"exited the tournament"] on Wednesday with a round-of-16 loss, and said the incident had left her drained. A study by the WTA and World Tennis showed players were subjected to over 12,000 abusive posts and messages on social media in 2025, up from 8,000 posts the previous year.

item.title: Abbas postpones Palestinian elections, sets presidential poll for September 2027
item.description: The Palestinian president blamed Israel, whose foreign minister rejected his remarks as a lie.
item.dc:creator: Ali Sawafta, Nidal Al-Mughrabi, Eman Abouhassira
item.content:encoded: Palestinian President Mahmoud Abbas on Saturday postponed legislative elections due next month until September 11, 2027, and called a presidential poll for the same date, blaming Israel and the security situation in the Palestinian territories for the delay. Abbas' decree cited "obstacles posed by Israeli measures" and the need to establish suitable political, security and on-the-ground conditions for "free, fair and inclusive elections", the official Palestinian news agency WAFA reported. In a post on X, Israeli Foreign Minister Gideon Saar, pointing to the last Palestinian election having been held two decades ago, rejected Abbas' remarks as "yet another ridiculous lie designed to evade responsibility and accountability." There had been serious doubts that the [USN:L8N45G1M5 TEXT:"Palestinian Authority vote"] would go ahead next month. The Palestinians have not held legislative or presidential elections since 2005-2006, after which Abbas' rival, the Islamist group Hamas, seized control of Gaza, ousting his loyalists. Abbas has governed by decree since his presidential mandate expired in 2009. The Palestinian Authority held municipal elections in April in the West Bank and in Deir al-Balah in central Gaza, the only city in the enclave to participate. The vote was the first election held in Gaza since 2006. The decree said Israeli military attacks, settlement expansion, settler violence and movement restrictions in the West Bank, including East Jerusalem, along with Israel's continued withholding of Palestinian tax revenues, created challenges to preparing for and holding elections this November. In Gaza , the decree pointed to "exceptional security and humanitarian conditions", the incomplete withdrawal of Israeli forces, the lack of progress in reconstruction and the failure to implement arrangements for deploying international stabilisation forces and police. The decree called on Palestinians in Jerusalem, the West Bank and Gaza to vote. Israeli restrictions on access for election commission staff and international observers to Gaza and East Jerusalem also complicated preparations, the decree said. Israel typically bans the Palestinian Authority from holding elections in East Jerusalem, territory it captured in the 1967 war and later annexed in a move most countries do not recognize. The decision to postpone followed consultations with Palestinian factions and political forces. It also aimed to allow time for a comprehensive Palestinian national dialogue to strengthen unity and address challenges facing the electoral process. PLEDGE TO HOLD VOTE AFTER TWO DECADES Two Palestinian officials told Reuters on Thursday that leaders of Abbas' Fatah movement and rival Hamas had agreed at a meeting in Cairo on Wednesday to postpone the elections. An August poll by the West Bank-based Palestinian Center for Policy and Survey Research (PSR) showed declining support for both Hamas and Fatah, which many Palestinians in Gaza and the West Bank blame for their continuing political divisions. The delay comes just weeks after Abbas reaffirmed the November election timetable in his September 24 address to the UN General Assembly, as he sought to advance internationally backed reforms. Abbas had committed in writing to French President Emmanuel Macron and Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman to hold presidential and legislative elections as part of France's recognition of a Palestinian state in September 2025. France's foreign ministry [USN:L1N45V090 TEXT:"said on Thursday"] that holding the elections was essential, and it welcomed the launch of an EU election observation mission.

item.title: Major Saudi conferences to proceed, organisers say, despite deadly airport attack
item.description: The organisers of two major Saudi energy and investment conferences said their events will go ahead this month and reassured visitors on security, after missile attacks on Riyadh's airport left four people dead and an airliner heavily damaged this week.
item.dc:creator: Timour Azhari, Federico Maccioni
item.content:encoded: The organisers of two major Saudi energy and investment conferences said their events will go ahead this month and reassured visitors on security, after [USN:L1N45V07H TEXT:"missile attacks"] on Riyadh's airport left four people dead and an airliner heavily damaged this week. The attacks led to widespread flight disruptions, with people taking land routes or circuitous alternative flights. The UK, France and Germany have warned their citizens to avoid Riyadh. Riyadh is sticking to plans to convene global events and trying to draw in investment even amid escalating war with the Iran-backed Houthis in neighbouring Yemen that has seen the kingdom attacked dozens of times over the past weeks. Organisers of the World Petroleum Congress, set to host top global oil executives and policymakers from Sunday to Thursday, said it would proceed as planned with foreign leaders and ministers in attendance, an email sent to delegates said. "Your comfort is our priority," it said, noting that alternative routes to Riyadh, including via a four-hour drive from Dammam on the kingdom's eastern coast, were available. Italian Energy Minister Gilberto Pichetto Fratin on Friday said he would not fly to Riyadh for the International Energy Forum Ministerial Meeting, an event on WPC's sidelines, but would participate via video link. The Future Investment Initiative, launched by Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman as the kingdom's flagship investment conference a decade ago, would also proceed as planned from October 26-29, organisers said. "Safety and well-being remain our highest priority," a statement attributed to FII CEO Maha Al Saud said. "Comprehensive security measures will be in place at Riyadh's airports, our conference venues and official hotels, with coordinated arrangements for participants' transportation," it said. Chief executives of some of the world's biggest financial institutions such as JPMorgan's Jamie Dimon and Citi's Jane Fraser were on the list of expected attendees. Citi and JPMorgan did not immediately respond to a request for comment. The Houthis have said airliners should avoid Saudi airspace, declaring it a zone of military operations after the Saudi-backed Yemeni government launched an offensive against the group earlier this month. Germany's Lufthansa has suspended Riyadh flights through October 16 while Gulf carriers Etihad Airways and Flydubai have cancelled flights to and from the Saudi capital scheduled for October 10. Saudi Arabia has responded to Houthi attacks with a wave of strikes on missile launcher sites, vowing to protect the kingdom, and says it has intercepted many ballistic missiles fired by the group.

item.title: Trump calls for replacing Ukraine's Zelenskiy in tussle over diesel deal with Russia
item.description: In some of his harshest criticism yet of the White House, Ukraine's president linked the US lifting of sanctions on Russian diesel with a Russian attack that killed 20 people, including three children, in Zaporizhzhia.
item.dc:creator: Max Hunder, Steve Holland
item.content:encoded: US President Donald Trump on Saturday called for Ukraine to replace its leader Volodymyr Zelenskiy and railed against Ukraine's attacks on Russian oil infrastructure, a day after announcing a diesel supply deal with Russia that had drawn a sharp rebuke from Zelenskiy. In some of his [USN:L1N45W01L TEXT:"harshest criticism"] yet of the White House, Zelenskiy linked the US lifting of sanctions on Russian diesel with a Russian attack on Saturday that killed 20 people, including 3 children, in the Ukrainian city of Zaporizhzhia. A steep rise in global diesel prices, which followed the outbreak of the Iran war in February, has become a political liability for Trump's Republican Party ahead of next month's midterm elections, when opposition Democrats could gain control of one or both houses of Congress. "I think it's time for Ukraine to get a new president," Trump told reporters at the White House, saying Zelenskiy had hurt global diesel supplies with strikes on Russian refineries. "He wants to make problems for our farmers, our ranchers, with diesel fuel because Russia supplies a large portion of the diesel fuel throughout the world." ZELENSKIY SAYS DIESEL DEAL EMBOLDENS RUSSIA Earlier in the day, Zelenskiy said Trump's announcement on Friday of the diesel deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin had emboldened Moscow. Kyiv has instead urged Washington to pressure Moscow for serious negotiations to end the 4-1/2-year-old war . The Russian government said on Saturday it had partially lifted a ban on diesel exports. "Today, Russia said thank you for the lifting of sanctions on diesel exports by dropping five glide bombs on residential buildings in Zaporizhzhia," Zelenskiy said. "Last night provided yet more confirmation that Russia perceives any easing of pressure as a signal that it can supposedly keep fighting, that it can supposedly keep dropping bombs on cities. Different signals are needed." The southern Ukrainian city of Zaporizhzhia has been a regular target of Russian bombardment with [USN:L6N44312E TEXT:"strikes intensifying"] in the past few months. On Saturday, a 6-year-old girl was among those killed in Zaporizhzhia when one strike reduced part of an apartment block to rubble. Her grandfather, Anatoliy Chumniy, stood sobbing over her body, laid on the ground in a white bag, after rescuers pulled it from the wreckage. "Her birthday would have been at the end of the month," he said through tears. It was the third mass-casualty attack on Ukraine this week. Nearly 80 civilians were killed in Russian strikes on Wednesday and Thursday, including at least 30 killed by a bomb in the eastern garrison city of Kramatorsk and 22 others by a missile in the town of Pryluky, about 130 km (80 miles) east of Kyiv. The diesel deal was also criticized by US lawmakers, including one of Trump's fellow Republicans, Representative Don Bacon, who said it was time to apply more sanctions that Congress had recently passed, not lift them. Analysts said the agreement was unlikely to lead to sustained lower fuel prices, with the volumes still much lower than what Russia usually exports when its refineries are not under attack. BRITAIN VOWS TO STRENGTHEN RUSSIA SANCTIONS British Prime Minister Andy Burnham spoke with Zelenskiy on Saturday and said [USN:FWN45V15A TEXT:"Britain would strengthen"] its sanctions on Russia, according to a Downing Street spokesperson, who added that the two leaders would meet in person in the coming days. The latest strikes followed talks between Ukrainian and European officials with US negotiators in Miami on Friday, which were aimed at developing a common [USN:L1N45V11A TEXT:"proposal for ending the war,"] according to a person familiar with the discussions. Trump announced the diesel deal while the negotiations were under way, a move Zelenskiy said had caught Kyiv by surprise. The Ukrainian delegation was headed home on Saturday, presidential aide Dmytro Lytvyn was cited by the Interfax Ukraine news agency as saying. Putin said after a call with Trump on Friday that an immediate resumption of peace talks was unlikely, citing Ukrainian drone attacks on Moscow. US negotiators Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner may visit Moscow within the next two weeks, Russian state news agency TASS reported on Saturday, citing a source. In his remarks at the White House, Trump criticized Zelenskiy over the lack of a peace deal, while demanding an end to Ukrainian strikes on Russian energy facilities. "I said to him, 'Do what you want. Don't hit refineries. There's plenty of targets. Don't hit refineries.' And he went out and he hit," Trump said. "He better damn well stop." "I suggest they get a new leader who can make a deal because he could have made many deals, but for some reason he never does," he added.

item.title: Isaias kills four, about 670,000 without power after landfall
item.description: The National Hurricane Center expects storm surges, flash flooding, damaging winds and a risk of tornadoes across parts of the US Southeast.
item.dc:creator: Rhea Abraham, Rajveer Pardesi, Marianna Parraga
item.content:encoded: Four people died after Hurricane Isaias made landfall early on Saturday, and about 670,000 residents in Florida, Alabama, Georgia and Mississippi were still without power as the storm weakened to a post-tropical cyclone, according to local authorities and electricity monitoring services. Two of the deaths resulted from trees falling on homes, according to local media and authorities. Authorities in Florida had received no search and rescue requests shortly after landfall in a sign of limited impact, Governor Ron DeSantis said. But hazardous conditions remained and storm surges, flash flooding, damaging winds and a risk of tornadoes across parts of the US Southeast were expected, the National Hurricane Center said. The tornado threat is expected to continue on Saturday across parts of the Florida Panhandle, Georgia and the Carolinas, the NHC said. In Florida, power restoration was marked as a priority, authorities said, while highways, bridges and airports were reopening, and teams were assessing the damage. "They're going to make assessments this morning, and I think that'll give us a good sense about the future for the rapidity of the power restoration," DeSantis told a press conference in Tallahassee. Some 16,000 utility linemen had prepared to respond to the storm, he said. About 420,000 customers in Florida, 190,000 in Alabama, 43,000 in Georgia and 17,000 in Mississippi had no power as of midday Saturday, according to tracking firm PowerOutage.us. A separate storm on the Pacific Ocean, Rachel, was moving toward the coast of northern Baja California on Saturday, bringing wind gusts and increased tides, which left another 7,000 people without power in California. Alabama's emergency management agency said the downed trees and power lines made travel hazardous in Houston County, which is under a flash flood warning. "Due to the impacts of Hurricane Isaias, all Houston County roads are closed until further notice," it posted on X. A category 2 hurricane when it hit Florida's coast and the first of the 2026 Atlantic season, Isaias is expected to produce gusty winds well inland before weakening below gale force later on Saturday, the NHC said. On Saturday, oil and gas producer Shell (SHEL.L) said it was beginning to redeploy personnel to its Mars, Olympus, Ursa, Vito and Appomattox assets in the Gulf, while Chevron (CVX.N) was advancing efforts to redeploy staff to its platforms and seeking to restore full production. "Remobilization of crews will continue through Sunday," it said. Despite the progress, about 69% of oil output and 57% of natural gas production in the US Gulf of Mexico remained shut on Saturday, slightly down from Friday numbers, the Marine Minerals Administration said. Some 113 production platforms representing 30% of the total remained evacuated, according to the agency. President Donald Trump, asked about hurricane preparations on Friday, told reporters outside the White House that it was "under control." The US Energy Department said on Saturday it authorized an emergency exchange of up to 4 million barrels of crude oil from the Strategic Petroleum Reserve to address supply disruptions due to the hurricane. Emergency declarations were approved in Florida and Alabama to ensure federal resources would be available to respond to Isaias, Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said on X. "There's also a lot of hazards post-storm that people should be careful of, but so far, we've had a lot of assets in place that have not been called on," DeSantis told FOX News early on Saturday. In the coastal city of Pensacola, a lack of drinking water is a problem, the mayor said. Pensacola airport, Florida's 10th largest, was damaged by the storm and is closed to commercial flights until further notice.

item.title: Erik Prince's forces suffer battlefield loss in Congo, former UFC fighter among wounded, sources say
item.description: Popular former UFC fighter Tim Kennedy was among the wounded in an ambush that killed or wounded at least 20 people deployed by Vectus Global.
item.dc:creator: Jessica Donati
item.content:encoded: Blackwater founder Erik Prince's forces suffered a major battlefield loss in eastern Democratic Republic of Congo in mid-September when enemy forces ambushed them, killing and wounding at least 20 people, including a popular former UFC fighter, sources close to the government and his company said. The frontline clash shows how Prince, an ally and supporter of US President Donald Trump, has taken on an expanded role in Congo through his company Vectus Global. The company, which also operates in Haiti and other parts of Africa, provides consulting and security services and previously [USN:L6N3XA0X0 TEXT:"helped Congo’s army"] secure the city of Uvira in South Kivu against Rwanda-backed rebels who control swathes of the east. A veteran special operator reported on his podcast earlier this week that former US Green Beret and Ultimate Fighting Championship contestant Tim Kennedy was injured in Congo. The involvement of Prince's forces and the number of casualties have not previously been reported. The attack in South Kivu on September 17 left about 20 dead and wounded, two sources working with Congo's government said. The dead included at least seven Congolese and a former member of New Zealand's Special Forces, while the wounded included Kennedy and another foreign contractor, the sources said. A Vectus Global representative declined to comment. The company has not previously suffered casualties in Congo, a source with direct knowledge of the operation said. One of the sources who works for Congo's government said that Rwandan forces backing the M23 rebels may have surprised them by tracking a drone used for surveillance operations to their location. Spokespeople for the Congolese and Rwandan governments and for the M23 did not immediately respond to requests for comment. Kennedy, the former mixed martial arts fighter, survived the attack with three gunshot wounds to the leg, three sources said, and is being treated at the Walter Reed National Military Medical Center in the suburbs of Washington. Kennedy has a popular podcast channel and millions of followers on social media. Trump is a fan of UFC, [USN:L6N42N00Z TEXT:"hosting fights"] at the White House this year. The US State Department and Walter Reed declined to comment. Kennedy's parents did not respond to requests for comment. A Congolese security source, who said some 20 people were wounded and killed in the attack, added that villagers were likely among the casualties as well. Reuters spoke to at least 10 sources either with direct knowledge of the attack or briefed on the outcome. PRINCE TOOK EXPANDED ROLE IN CONGO'S CONFLICT Prince's initial mandate in Congo was to secure and improve revenue collection from the country's vast mineral reserves, which have been plundered for decades, fuelling relentless conflict in the east. But in January and early February, his forces deployed to Uvira after Washington helped broker a deal for Rwandan-backed rebels to withdraw from the strategic town. The size of Prince's forces in Congo is unclear. One of the sources with direct knowledge of the attack said the Vectus team was travelling between locations when the ambush took place and its sophistication suggested Rwandan forces were involved. "It reinforces the need for DRC sovereignty to be restored. It's an incredibly dangerous place right now," the source said. Two other sources said the ambush was carried out by the Rwandan military. Prince is the founder of now-defunct private military firm Blackwater, some of whose members were pardoned in 2020 for killing Iraqi civilians. The State Department has said it does not have any contracts with Prince in Congo, though US officials have said they plan to work [USN:L1N43O0RW TEXT:"more closely with Vectus Global"] in Haiti. The deal for Rwandan-backed rebels to withdraw from Uvira was part of [USN:L6N3XA0X0 TEXT:"wider agreements"] brokered by the Trump administration to try to end the conflict in eastern Congo. POPULAR PODCASTER Kennedy, a father of four, has posted his views on politics, culture, fitness and more on social media. He also runs a popular YouTube podcast in which he interviews UFC fighters, veterans, cultural disruptors and others. He has often posted about his family, including four young children. In late August, he posted about having "incredible conversations about what being a man means and what sacrifice really looks like" with his son. He did not disclose details about his upcoming trip to Congo. The United Nations and Western powers say Rwanda backs M23, even exercising command and control over the group. Rwanda denies this. Fighting in the decades-long conflict flared early last year, with M23 fighters making rapid gains in the east, which is rich in tantalum, gold, lithium and other minerals.

item.title: Anthropic discloses fake tip to police among new rogue AI incidents
item.description: "I may have information regarding this case."
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: An Anthropic artificial intelligence model submitted a false homicide tip to a Philadelphia police website, among a string of incidents the AI company disclosed on Friday detailing Claude models' unsanctioned manipulation of some government websites. It is the first known instance in which a rogue AI appears to have tried to communicate a bogus tip to authorities, despite instructions not to create accounts or submit anything destructive, while not explicitly barred from submitting forms. The cases are the latest examples of rogue or undesired behavior by the AI models of tech companies such as Anthropic and OpenAI. They add fuel to national concerns about the fast-advancing technology amid reports of corporate network hacks by AI agents, and researchers' warnings of an eventual existential threat to humanity. Many of the cases Anthropic revealed involved websites run by federal, state and local agencies. Anthropic said it briefed the White House and notified all the agencies involved, but did not disclose who those parties were. "Super intelligence companies must immediately disclose incidents involving their models and follow with swift, decisive action to remedy any and all harm," FTC Director of Public Affairs Joe Gabriel Simonson said on X. This process was "not optional," he said, adding that the Super Intelligence Force would fulfill its responsibility. The FTC said Anthropic disclosed to the SI Force on Friday its late September discovery of incidents involving what the task force called "unauthorized and fraudulent use of government and other systems". TIP ATTRIBUTED TO AUTOMATED TEST PROCESS On Friday, Philadelphia police said Anthropic notified them of the spurious tip this week, and attributed the submissions to an automated testing process. "The two-month delay in detecting and reporting the incident to the city is unacceptable," they said. The July 18 tip purported to come from someone who might have information about the case, police added. "I may have information regarding this case," Anthropic's model wrote in its submission. "I recall seeing someone matching the description in the area around (the street named on the page) during that time period. Please contact me if this information is relevant." The brackets featured in Anthropic's statement. Previous incidents have involved AI agents hacking into vulnerable systems or commandeering unsanctioned platforms to communicate with one another. In September, Anthropic rival OpenAI apologized for the hacking of an Australian health data portal by a rogue AI agent, the first known instance of an AI agent exploiting a government website. A BOGUS TIP In two cases described on Friday, Anthropic’s models obtained for free public data normally only available for a fee. Another instanced revealed an obscure flaw that allowed use of a public tool hosted by a university. Claude models were also able to bypass restrictions by using free services that shorten URLs. Philadelphia police said the tip "was flagged as spam and was never forwarded to the Real-Time Crime Center for investigative vetting or dissemination." Knowingly giving false reports to law enforcement authorities is a misdemeanor under Pennsylvania law, which specifies "a person", however. This includes "information relating to an offense or incident when he knows he has no information relating to such offense or incident." Police quoted Anthropic as telling them the test process was stopped after discovery of the incident. The false tip was submitted through PhillyUnsolvedMurders.com concerning an unsolved homicide. Police said they had no evidence of unauthorized access to their systems or compromise of their data.

item.title: Wall St Week Ahead Bank earnings, CPI headline busy markets week as S&P 500 hovers near records
item.description: Quarterly earnings reports from banks, along with inflation data and other economic releases next week, will offer US stock investors insight into the strength of corporate profits and the path of interest rates, two factors influencing the market's rally.
item.dc:creator: Lewis Krauskopf
item.content:encoded: Quarterly earnings reports from banks, along with inflation data and other economic releases next week, will offer US stock investors insight into the strength of corporate profits and the path of interest rates, two factors influencing the market's rally. On Tuesday, the S&P 500 (.SPX) hit an all-time closing high, its first since mid-August. Its year-to-date gain has swelled to more than 14%. Wednesday's Consumer Price Index report, perhaps the most closely watched inflation gauge, is among the last key data releases before the Federal Reserve meets at the end of October to decide whether to raise interest rates. The Fed hiked rates last month for the first time since 2023 to try to contain inflation. Banks including JPMorgan (JPM.N) and Goldman Sachs (GS.N) [USN:L1N45R0GT TEXT:"will report next week"], kicking off what is expected to be an exceptionally strong quarter overall for [USN:L6N45K12P TEXT:"US corporate profits"]. Following a robust first half, S&P 500 earnings are expected to have jumped by more than 30% in the third quarter, according to LSEG IBES. "Earnings have been incredible this year, and we're just going to have to start to see with the banks how Q3 shaped up," said Matthew Miskin, co-chief investment strategist at Manulife John Hancock Investments. BANKS TO GIVE VIEWS ON CONSUMER, CAPITAL MARKETS JPMorgan, Goldman, Citigroup (C.N) and Wells Fargo (WFC.N) will report results on Tuesday. Morgan Stanley (MS.N) and Bank of America (BAC.N) are set to report the following day, rounding out reports from the six largest banks. Banks typically kick off quarterly earnings season, and the reports offer important views into the health of the overall US economy. Matt Stucky, chief portfolio manager of equities at Northwestern Mutual Wealth Management, said he would focus on how higher interest rates are rippling through to capital markets and consumer spending. "We've seen rates back up. We've seen energy costs back up," Stucky said. "And the question is, how is this impacting the consumer?" Heading into the reports, bank stocks have been among the worst-performing groups recently amid a rise in Treasury yields, with the S&P 500 banks index (.SPXBK) down 7.5% in the past month. "Is the market sniffing out something that is underneath the surface for these financial companies?" Miskin said. "I think there's going to be a sigh of relief if these financial services companies come out with good results next week." Other earnings reports next week include healthcare companies Johnson & Johnson (JNJ.N) and UnitedHealth Group (UNH.N) , and asset manager BlackRock (BLK.N) . COULD CPI REVIVE RATE-HIKE BETS? Wednesday's September CPI report is expected to show a 3.7% rise on an annual basis, according to a Reuters poll. The core measure, excluding volatile energy and food components, is estimated to increase by a more modest 2.5%. The Fed targets a 2% annual inflation rate. Michael Reynolds, vice president of investment strategy at Glenmede, said he was concerned with "sticky" services inflation that has been showing up in reports. "We really want to see material progress on (core services inflation) to get a little bit more confident that the Fed doesn't have to be as aggressive as maybe the market's pricing in," Reynolds said. Reports next week on producer prices and retail sales will give a fuller picture of the economy. Traders have reduced expectations the Fed will increase rates again at its October 27-28 meeting. But data that shows a hotter economy could revive hiking bets, investors said. "If you start to see more evidence of re-accelerating inflation that's not going to come down absent a full hiking cycle from the Fed, that's where equity markets really can be under pressure," Stucky said. The Fed's move to start hiking rates has been one factor pushing Treasury yields higher. The benchmark 10-year yield was around 5.24% late on Friday, after recently reaching its highest level in 24 years. Higher yields pose a number of obstacles for equity performance, including by making bonds more competitive investments and by pressuring stock valuations. While a 5% yield on the 10-year Treasury had been seen as a key threshold to create stock pressure, the market has avoided any significant downside thus far as yields have breached that level and then moved even higher. "At some point, major indices are going to cry uncle on higher rates," Reynolds said.

item.title: OFRBS Summary
item.description: La célèbre 2CV reprend du service ... en électrique
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: La célèbre 2CV reprend du service ... en électrique VELIZY/MEUDON, 11 octobre (Reuters) - Stellantis a dévoilé dimanche un concept car très attendu, préfigurant le retour de la 2CV Citroën, une icône dont le groupe a choisi de reprendre de nombreux codes pour se distinguer d'une concurrence toujours plus nombreuse en Europe. Wall Street termine la semaine en hausse La Bourse de New York a clôturé en hausse vendredi dans l'attente du coup d'envoi de la saison des résultats trimestriels et de la publication des chiffres mensuels de l'inflation la semaine prochaine. L'Europe finit en hausse, le CAC 40 pénalisé par l'incertitude budgétaire Les Bourses européennes ont terminé en hausse vendredi, mais le CAC 40 termine sur une nette baisse hebdomadaire, la situation budgétaire en France restant sous vigilance, tandis que l'accalmie sur les cours pétroliers s'estompe. La Chine et l'UE parviennent s'entendent sur les véhicules hybrides La Chine et l'Union européenne sont parvenues à un "accord" sur le commerce des véhicules hybrides, a annoncé vendredi le ministère chinois du Commerce, à l'issue de deux jours de négociations au cours desquelles l'UE a cherché à réduire son déficit commercial avec Pékin. Delta Air Lines abaisse ses prévisions de bénéfices, avec la hausse des coûts du carburant Delta Air Lines a réduit sa prévision de bénéfice annuel de près 25% vendredi, l'impact de la flambée des prix du carburant annulant à la fois la forte demande de voyages et la hausse des prix des billets. La BCE pourrait devoir procéder à de nouvelles hausses de taux, estime Dolenc La Banque centrale européenne (BCE) pourrait être contrainte de continuer à relever ses taux directeurs face au risque d'une aggravation de l'inflation mais le moment et l'ampleur d'une telle mesure restent bien trop incertains pour pouvoir être prédits, a déclaré Primož Dolenc, membre du Conseil des gouverneurs de l'institution de Francfort et gouverneur de la banque centrale slovène. L'AIE appelle à envisager un nouveau recours aux stocks stratégiques 11 octobre (Reuters) - Le directeur exécutif de l'Agence internationale de l'énergie (AIE), Fatih Birol, a proposé dimanche que tous les pays membres réfléchissent à la nécessité de procéder à des libérations supplémentaires des stocks de diesel et en définissent l'ampleur, le calendrier et le caractère complémentaire. Le secteur du luxe freiné davantage par des mesures fiscales en Chine Le tour de vis enclenché par la Chine pour lutter contre l'évasion fiscale des plus fortunés est devenu un motif supplémentaire d'inquiétude pour les enseignes de luxe, lesquelles font déjà face aux répercussions de la guerre en Iran et à un ralentissement de la consommation aux Etats-Unis. Le gouvernement allemand relève ses prévisions de croissance pour 2026 et 2027 Le gouvernement allemand a revu à la hausse ses prévisions économiques pour cette année et l'année prochaine, la guerre en Iran n'ayant pas un impact aussi sévère qu'initialement redouté, a déclaré jeudi le ministère de l'Economie. Zone euro: Les rendements obligataires se tendent encore Les rendements obligataires de la zone euro enregistrent jeudi de nouvelles fortes tensions, dans un contexte de hausse des prix de l'énergie, les investisseurs continuant à se débarrasser des obligations des pays les plus endettés comme la France et l'Italie, provoquant un creusement des "spreads" dans le bloc.

item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: Ukraine-Trump annonce un cessez-le-feu dans l'énergie, Zelensky attend des précisions KYIV, 11 octobre (Reuters) - Le président américain Donald Trump a annoncé dimanche la conclusion d'un accord de cessez-le-feu entre l'Ukraine et la Russie portant sur les infrastructures énergétiques et son entrée en vigueur, avant d'être rapidement contredit par son homologue ukrainien Volodimir Zelensky. Au moins 139 migrants périssent dans un naufrage au large de Djibouti 11 octobre (Reuters) - Au moins 139 migrants, dont 15 enfants, ont péri et environ 84 autres sont portés disparus après le naufrage d'une embarcation transportant 305 personnes entre Djibouti et le Yémen, a annoncé dimanche l'Organisation internationale pour les migrations (OIM), une agence des Nations unies. L'aéroport de Ryad a encore été ciblé, dit la coalition dirigée par l'Arabie saoudite DUBAI/RYAD 11 octobre (Reuters) - La coalition dirigée par l'Arabie saoudite au Yémen a annoncé qu'un "projectile non identifié" avait frappé dimanche l'aéroport international de Ryad, provoquant un incendie, au lendemain d'une attaque contre ce même aéroport revendiquée par les Houthis qui a fait 12 morts. Le pape Léon va être opéré d'un nodule au poumon CITE DU VATICAN, 11 octobre (Reuters) - Le pape Léon a déclaré dimanche que les médecins avaient détecté une petite excroissance pulmonaire lors d'un récent examen de santé et qu'il subirait une intervention chirurgicale cette semaine pour la retirer. GB-Burnham dit que la Russie s'est ingérée dans le référendum sur le Brexit de 2016 LONDRES, 11 octobre (Reuters) - La Russie s'est ingérée dans le référendum sur le Brexit de 2016, a déclaré le Premier ministre britannique Andy Burnham lors d'un entretien diffusé dimanche, en mettant en garde la France et l'Allemagne contre les tentatives soutenues par Moscou visant à influencer leur vie politique. L'Iran dit que la réponse des USA à sa proposition de rouvrir Ormuz était "insuffisante" DUBAÏ, 11 octobre (Reuters) - La réponse des États-Unis aux conditions posées par l'Iran dans le cadre d'une proposition visant à rouvrir le détroit d'Ormuz a été jugée "insuffisante", a déclaré dimanche le chef de la sécurité iranienne, Mohsen Rezaei, cité par les médias d'État. Le Népal exhorte des villageois à évacuer après une inondation provoquée par un glissement de terrain KATMANDOU, 11 octobre (Reuters) - Les autorités népalaises ont exhorté dimanche des villageois à se mettre à l'abri après que plusieurs maisons et infrastructures ont été emportées par l'importante crue d'une rivière dans le centre du pays. Pologne-Un homme arrêté après des menaces visant le Premier ministre VARSOVIE, 11 octobre (Reuters) - La police polonaise a interpellé un homme soupçonné d'avoir préparé une attaque contre le Premier ministre Donald Tusk, a annoncé dimanche le ministre de l'Intérieur, après avoir fait état de menaces visant Donald Tusk et le ministre de la Défense Wladyslaw Kosiniak-Kamysz. L'armée américaine met hors d'usage un navire dans le golfe d'Oman 10 octobre (Reuters) - L'armée américaine a déclaré samedi avoir mis hors d'usage un navire commercial dans le Golfe d'Oman après que l'équipage, ignorant des avertissements, a tenté de forcer le blocus naval imposé par les Etats-Unis contre l'Iran. Une nouvelle attaque contre l'aéroport de Ryad fait douze morts, selon des sources RYAD, 10 octobre (Reuters) - Une attaque contre l'aéroport de Ryad a fait douze morts et des dizaines de blessés samedi, selon trois sources au fait du dossier, tandis que tous les vols ont été déroutés.

item.content:encoded: Raphaël Glucksmann remporte la primaire social-démocrate dès le premier tour PARIS, 11 octobre (Reuters) - Le candidat Place Publique à l'élection présidentielle, Raphaël Glucksmann, a remporté dès le premier tour la primaire social-démocrate, a annoncé dimanche le Parti socialiste. La France appelle les autorités palestiniennes à revenir sur le report les élections PARIS, 11 octobre (Reuters) - La France regrette le report par le président palestinien Mahmoud Abbas des élections législatives et présidentielle, a déclaré dimanche un porte-parole du ministère des Affaires étrangères, appelant les autorités palestiniennes à revenir sur cette décision. Nobel/Littérature: Le prix décerné à la poète et écrivaine canadienne Anne Carson Le prix Nobel de littérature a été décerné jeudi à la poète et écrivaine canadienne Anne Carson pour "son oeuvre audacieuse et inventive qui, dans un dialogue ludique avec la tradition classique, a créé de nouvelles formes pour la littérature contemporaine", a annoncé jeudi l'Académie royale des sciences de Suède. Les deux Renoir dérobés au musée de Cagnes-sur-Mer retrouvés Les deux tableaux dérobés il y a un peu plus d'un mois au musée Renoir de Cagnes-sur-Mer (Alpes-Maritimes) ont été retrouvés par la police et six suspects ont été arrêtés, a déclaré vendredi le maire Rassemblement national (RN) de la ville, Bryan Masson. L'Allemagne abandonne le projet de char commun avec la France-Mandon L'Allemagne a décidé d'abandonner le projet avec la France de char commun du futur, le MGCS ("Main Ground Combat System", système principal de combat terrestre), a annoncé jeudi le chef d'état-major des armées, Fabien Mandon, lors d'une audition devant une commission parlementaire. France-Dix millions de barils de gazole libérés des réserves pour baisser les prix à la pompe-Lecornu La France va libérer 10 millions de barils de gazole de ses réserves stratégiques avec l'objectif d'agir sur les prix à la pompe, qui devraient ainsi "mécaniquement baisser" de 12 centimes à 18 centimes d'euro par litre de gazole, a déclaré mercredi soir le Premier ministre Sébastien Lecornu. Le Danemark accuse la Russie d'actes de sabotage contre ses entreprises du secteur de la défense La Russie a lancé des opérations de sabotage contre des entreprises danoises fournissant l'Ukraine après avoir conclu que ses tentatives de perturbation à plus grande échelle n'avaient pas freiné le soutien militaire occidental à Kyiv, a déclaré mercredi une responsable des services de renseignement danois. Nuñez suspend l'usage des grenades assourdissantes contre les lycéens L'usage des grenades assourdissantes par les forces de l'ordre est suspendu "dans le cadre du mouvement lycéen", a annoncé mercredi sur RTL le ministre de l'Intérieur, Laurent Nuñez. De plus en plus d'enfants non accompagnés empruntent des voies dangereuses pour rejoindre l'Europe, selon l'Onu Plus des deux tiers des enfants réfugiés et migrants qui ont rejoint l'Europe par les routes de la Méditerranée et des Balkans en 2025 étaient non accompagnés et bon nombre d'entre eux ont été victimes d'exploitation, selon un rapport publié mercredi par des agences des Nations Unies. La France ne peut plus se permettre la moindre erreur sur ses finances publiques dit Citadel La France ne peut plus se permettre la moindre erreur dans l'assainissement de ses finances publiques et la pression exercée par les marchés devrait inciter le gouvernement à se concentrer sur la maîtrise des dépenses à l'approche de l'élection présidentielle de 2027, a déclaré à Reuters Angel Ubide, économiste chez la société de gestion d'actifs Citadel.
